chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter starts from a carpenter's problem: how must two wooden strips be joined so that a thread through their ends makes a rectangle? Answering it needs deductions, and each later family (square, parallelogram, rhombus, kite, trapezium) is met the same way: define it, predict a property, prove it with congruent triangles or parallel lines, then check it by constructing and measuring.

points.title: Predict, then prove
points.text: Every concept opens with a question the student answers first, such as whether the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal, and then a short deduction settles it.

points.title: Measuring makes a conjecture, reasoning makes it sure
points.text: Constructions and measurements suggest a property; only a deduction shows it holds for every quadrilateral of that kind.

points.title: One shape, several names
points.text: A square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and every rhombus is a parallelogram and a kite. Venn diagrams make the family visible.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Ten tools, each used once: crossing strips, dragging a quadrilateral, a square in a square, tearing and placing the four angles, sides and angles, a hinged rhombus, diagonals, sliding kites and trapeziums, and sorting figures into the family rings.

concepts.concept_name: What makes a figure a quadrilateral?

content.text:
In this chapter, we will study some interesting types of four-sided figures and solve problems based on them. Such figures are commonly known as quadrilaterals. The word 'quadrilateral' is derived from Latin words, quadri meaning four, and latus referring to sides.
Observe the following figures.
Figs. (i), (ii), and (iii) are quadrilaterals, and the others are not. Why?
The angles of a quadrilateral are the angles between its sides, as marked in Figs. (i), (ii), and (iii).
We will start with the most familiar quadrilaterals, rectangles and squares.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a carpenter's workshop is full of frames. Which of them are quadrilaterals, and which are not?
2. A quadrilateral is a closed figure made of exactly four straight sides that meet only at their ends.
3. A figure with a curved side, an open gap, or more than four sides is not a quadrilateral.
4. The angles of a quadrilateral are the four angles between its sides, one at each corner.
5. Keep this question open: the carpenter wants a frame that is exactly rectangular. How can she be sure it is?

modules.module_summary: A rectangle defined three ways: by its angles and sides, by its diagonals, and by its angles alone. Its diagonals are equal and bisect each other, its opposite sides are equal and parallel, and the square is the special rectangle whose diagonals also meet at right angles and bisect its angles.

segments.summary: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other. Conversely, two equal strips joined at their midpoints, at any angle, always give a rectangle, so a rectangle can be defined by its diagonals.

concepts.concept_name: The Carpenter's Problem: the other strip

content.text:
4.1 Rectangles and Squares
Rectangle: A rectangle is a quadrilateral in which (i) The angles are all right angles (90°), and (ii) The opposite sides are of equal length.
Are there other ways to define a rectangle?
A carpenter needs to put together two thin strips of wood so that when a thread is passed through their endpoints, it forms a rectangle. She already has one 8 cm long strip. What should be the length of the other strip? Where should they both be joined?
1. What is the length of the other diagonal? 2. What is the point of intersection of the two diagonals? 3. What should the angle be between the diagonals?
Since ABCD is a rectangle, we have AB = CD, ∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90°, and AD is common to both triangles. So, ∆ADC ≅ ∆DAB by the SAS congruence condition.
Therefore, AC = BD. This shows that the diagonals of a rectangle always have the same length.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the carpenter has one strip of 8 cm. Should the other strip be shorter, longer, or the same?
2. The strips are the diagonals of the quadrilateral their ends make. Suppose the ends already form a rectangle ABCD.
3. Compare ∆ADC and ∆DAB: AB = CD, the angles at A and D are both 90°, and AD is shared. SAS makes them congruent.
4. So AC = BD: the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal. The other strip must also be 8 cm.

content.text:
Worked example: The carpenter has one strip 8 cm long. How long must the other strip be for the thread to make a rectangle?
1. Model the strips as the diagonals AC and BD of a rectangle ABCD, with AC = 8 cm.
2. In ∆ADC and ∆DAB: AB = CD, ∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90°, and AD is a common side.
3. By the SAS condition, ∆ADC ≅ ∆DAB.
4. So AC = BD, as corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
5. The other strip must be 8 cm long.
Answer: 8 cm, because the diagonals of a rectangle are equal

concepts.concept_name: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other

content.text:
Deduction 2: What is the point of intersection of the two diagonals?
The blue angles are equal since they are vertically opposite angles. In order to show congruence, consider ∠1 and ∠2. Are they equal?
Since ∠B is a right angle, ∠1 and ∠3 together make a right angle. In ∆BCD, ∠3 and ∠2 together also make a right angle, because ∠C is a right angle. So, ∠1 = ∠2, each being 90° minus ∠3.
Thus, by the AAS condition for congruence, ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD. Hence OA = OC and OB = OD.
When the diagonals cross at their midpoints, we say that the diagonals bisect each other. Bisecting a quantity means dividing it into two equal parts.
Can the following equalities be used to establish that ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB? AO = CO (proved above), ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite angles), AD = CB.

1. Predict first: where must the two strips cross, at their middles or somewhere else?
2. Look at ∆AOB and ∆COD: AB = CD, the angles at O are vertically opposite, and ∠1 = ∠2 because each is 90° − ∠3.

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and AC = 8 cm. Find OA, OC, OB and OD.
1. In ∆AOB and ∆COD: AB = CD, ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite), and ∠ABD = ∠CDB (each is 90° minus the same angle).
2. By the AAS condition, ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD, so OA = OC and OB = OD.
3. The diagonals are equal, so BD = AC = 8 cm.
4. Each half is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.
Answer: OA = OC = OB = OD = 4 cm; the strips are joined at their midpoints

concepts.concept_name: Equal diagonals that bisect each other make a rectangle

content.text:
Deduction 3: What are the angles between the diagonals?
Let us check what quadrilateral we get if we draw the two diagonals such that their lengths are equal, they bisect each other and have an arbitrary angle, say 60°, between them. Can you find all the remaining angles?
In ∆AOB, since OA = OB, the angles opposite them are equal, say a. a + a + 60 = 180. Therefore 2a = 120. Thus a = 60.
We can see that ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD and ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB. Hence, AB = CD, and AD = CB. Therefore, ABCD is a rectangle.
Carpenters in Europe use this method to get a rectangular frame. Farmers in Mozambique, a country in Africa, use this method while constructing houses to get the base of the house in a rectangular shape.
The Process of Finding Properties: observations through measurement give useful insights, but with them we can only form a conjecture, a statement about which we are highly confident, but not yet sure if it always holds true. The only way we can be sure is by justifying or proving the statement.
Note to the Teacher: Gently encourage students to deduce or justify properties. Whenever students face challenges, encourage them to experiment and observe, and use their intuition.

lines: Deduction 3: What are the angles between the diagonals?

Let us check what quadrilateral we get if we draw the two diagonals such that their lengths are equal, they bisect each other and have an arbitrary angle, say 60°, between them. Can you find all the remaining angles?
In ∆AOB, since OA = OB, the angles opposite them are equal, say a. a + a + 60 = 180. Therefore 2a = 120. Thus a = 60.
We can see that ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD and ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB. Hence, AB = CD, and AD = CB. Therefore, ABCD is a rectangle.

Carpenters in Europe use this method to get a rectangular frame. Farmers in Mozambique, a country in Africa, use this method while constructing houses to get the base of the house in a rectangular shape.

The Process of Finding Properties: observations through measurement give useful insights, but with them we can only form a conjecture, a statement about which we are highly confident, but not yet sure if it always holds true. The only way we can be sure is by justifying or proving the statement.
Note to the Teacher: Gently encourage students to deduce or justify properties. Whenever students face challenges, encourage them to experiment and observe, and use their intuition.

content.text:
1. Predict first: two equal strips cross at their midpoints at 60°. Will the thread make a rectangle, or some slanted shape?
2. The angles at O are 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°, by vertically opposite angles and linear pairs.
3. All four half-diagonals are equal, so each small triangle is isosceles: the 60° triangles have base angles 60°, the 120° triangles have base angles 30°.
4. Every corner is 60° + 30° = 90°, and congruent triangles give equal opposite sides: a rectangle.
5. Carpenters in Europe and farmers in Mozambique use exactly this to set out rectangles.
6. Measuring many rectangles only gives a conjecture; this deduction is what makes us sure.

content.text:
Worked example: Two equal diagonals bisect each other and meet at 60°. Find all the angles of the quadrilateral ABCD and say what it is.
1. The four angles at O are 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°.
2. In ∆AOB, OA = OB, so its two base angles are equal. Their sum is 180 − 60 = 120, so each is 120 ÷ 2 = 60.
3. In ∆AOD the angle at O is 120°, so its base angles add to 180 − 120 = 60, and each is 30.
4. Each corner of ABCD is made of one angle of each kind: 60 + 30 = 90.
5. ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD and ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB by SAS, so AB = CD and AD = CB.
Answer: Every angle of ABCD is 90° and its opposite sides are equal, so ABCD is a rectangle

concepts.concept_name: Any angle between the diagonals

content.text:
Take one of the angles between the diagonals as x. We can compute the four angles between the diagonals to be x, x, 180 − x, and 180 − x.
a = (180 − x)/2 = 90 − x/2. Similarly, in the isosceles ∆AOD, let the base angles be b. b = x/2.
All the angles of the quadrilateral are a + b, which is 90 − x/2 + x/2 = 90.
Hence, no matter what the angles between the diagonals are, if the diagonals are equal and they bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a rectangle.

content.text:
Worked example: Equal diagonals bisect each other at 40°. Find the angles of the quadrilateral.
1. In the triangle with 40° at O, the base angles add to 180 − 40 = 140, so each is 140 ÷ 2 = 70.
2. The next triangle has 180 − 40 = 140 at O, so its base angles add to 180 − 140 = 40, and each is 20.
3. Each corner of the quadrilateral is 70 + 20 = 90.
Answer: All four angles are 90°, so it is again a rectangle

The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other.
Equal diagonals that bisect each other, at any angle, always make a rectangle.
Measuring suggests a property; a deduction proves it.

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 2): Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm that bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of (i) 30° (ii) 40° (iii) 90° (iv) 140°.
1. Draw AC = 8 cm and mark its midpoint O, so OA = OC = 4 cm.
2. At O draw a line making the given angle with OC.
3. On this line mark B and D on opposite sides of O with OB = OD = 4 cm, so BD = 8 cm.
4. Join A, B, C and D in order.
5. The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so each figure is a rectangle; at 90° all four sides are also equal.
Answer: All four are rectangles; the one with diagonals at 90° is a square

tool_config.idea: Two strips joined at their midpoints make a rectangle when they are equal, whatever angle they cross at: the angle changes the shape of the rectangle but never its corners. Unequal strips, or a joint off the middle, break it.

Set the lengths, the joint and the crossing angle.
Read the four corners and the four sides.
Change one thing at a time and see which change breaks the rectangle.

media.title: What shape do two equal crossing strips make at sixty degrees?
media.context: Quadrilaterals. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two equal strips cut each other in half and cross at sixty degrees. Angles in two isosceles triangles give every angle of the shape, and Keeko then doubts that equal angles must mean a square.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: equal diagonals that cut each other in half always give four right angles and equal opposite sides, so the shape is a rectangle. Watch for students who think four equal angles must mean four equal sides.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child sees why equal diagonals that cut each other in half always give a rectangle, by finding every angle once for a sixty degree crossing.

video_script.why: The child sees why equal diagonals that cut each other in half always give a rectangle, by finding every angle once for a sixty degree crossing.
video_script.substitution: Find the angles at O, then the base angles of two isosceles triangles, add one of each at every corner, and match triangles for the opposite sides.
video_script.anchor: quadrilateral ABCD whose equal diagonals AC and BD cross at O with 60 degrees between them
video_script.wrong_answer: it must be a square
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the shape must be a square because all four angles are equal; but side AD faces the 120 degree angle and is longer than side AB.
video_script.payoff_line: Every corner is ninety degrees and the shape is a rectangle

final_answer.spoken: every corner is ninety degrees and the shape is a rectangle

maths_rules: AC = BD and O is the midpoint of both, so OA = OB = OC = OD
angle AOB = angle COD = 60 degrees (vertically opposite); angle AOD = angle BOC = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees (linear pair)
triangle AOB with OA = OB: base angles add to 180 - 60 = 120, so each is 120 / 2 = 60 degrees
triangle AOD with OA = OD: base angles add to 180 - 120 = 60, so each is 60 / 2 = 30 degrees
each corner is 60 + 30 = 90 degrees, so all four angles are 90 degrees
SAS: triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COD and triangle AOD is congruent to triangle COB, so AB = CD and AD = CB
triangle AOB has three 60 degree angles, so AB = OA; AD faces the 120 degree angle, so AD > OA = AB; the shape is not a square
video_script.design: One idea: equal diagonals that bisect each other make a rectangle. Wrong idea: all four angles equal means a square. The figure with O and the sixty degree angle stays on the board.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students state the definition of a rectangle, model the carpenter's strips as diagonals, and prove by the SAS condition that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal.
Students prove by the AAS condition that the diagonals of a rectangle meet at their midpoints, and judge whether a given set of equalities is enough for a congruence.

Students find every angle of a quadrilateral whose equal diagonals bisect each other at 60°, show it is a rectangle, and explain the difference between a conjecture from measuring and a property proved by deduction.
Students repeat the argument with an angle of x between the diagonals and show every corner is still 90°.
Students construct quadrilaterals from equal diagonals that bisect each other at a given angle and use the same idea to make an exact right angle with two sticks and a thread.

concepts.concept_name: Rectangles and Squares, Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 4): We have seen how to get 90° using paper folding. Now, suppose we do not have any paper but two sticks of equal length, and a thread. How do we make an exact 90° using these?
1. Cross the two equal sticks so that their midpoints meet at O.
2. Pass the thread round the four ends of the sticks in order.
3. The sticks are equal diagonals that bisect each other, so the thread makes a rectangle.
4. Every corner of a rectangle is 90°, so the thread turns through an exact 90° at each stick end.
Answer: Cross the sticks at their midpoints and run the thread round the four ends; each corner of the thread is exactly 90°

content.text:
1. Predict first: can you draw four right angles whose opposite sides are not equal?
2. Join the diagonal BD. ∠A = ∠C = 90°, BD is shared, and ∠ABD = ∠CDB because each is 90° minus ∠DBC.
3. AAS gives ∆BAD ≅ ∆DCB, so the opposite sides are equal: four right angles are enough.
4. Write the letters in matching order: A goes with C (both 90°), so ∆BAD ≅ ∆CDB is wrong.

content.text:
Worked example: ABCD has all four angles 90°. Show that AD = CB and DC = BA, and say why writing ∆BAD ≅ ∆CDB is wrong.
1. Join the diagonal BD.
2. ∠BAD = ∠DCB = 90°, and BD is common to ∆BAD and ∆DCB.
3. ∠ABD + ∠DBC = 90° and ∠CDB + ∠DBC = 90°, so ∠ABD = ∠CDB.
4. By AAS, ∆BAD ≅ ∆DCB, matching B with D, A with C and D with B.
5. So AD = CB and BA = DC.
6. ∆CDB would match A with D, but the right angle at A matches the right angle at C, not D.
Answer: AD = CB and DC = BA; ∆BAD ≅ ∆CDB is wrong because the vertices are not in matching order

concepts.concept_name: Opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel

content.text:
Property 1: All the angles of a rectangle are 90°.
Property 2: The opposite sides of a rectangle are equal.
Are the opposite sides of a rectangle parallel? AB acts as a transversal to AD and BC, and ∠A + ∠B = 90° + 90° = 180°. When the sum of the internal angles on the same side of the transversal is 180°, the lines are parallel. So AD || BC.
Can you similarly show that AB is parallel to DC (AB||DC)?
Property 3: The opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel to each other.
Property 4: The diagonals of a rectangle are of equal length and they bisect each other.

content.text:
1. Predict first: are the opposite sides of a rectangle parallel, and how could you be sure without measuring?
2. Take a side as a transversal: the two angles on the same side of it are 90° and 90°, adding to 180°.
3. Internal angles on the same side adding to 180° means the lines are parallel.
4. So a rectangle has all angles 90°, opposite sides equal, opposite sides parallel, and equal diagonals that bisect each other.

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle ABCD, show that AB is parallel to DC.
1. Take AD as a transversal to the lines AB and DC.
2. The internal angles on the same side of AD are ∠A and ∠D.
3. ∠A + ∠D = 90 + 90 = 180.
4. Internal angles on the same side of a transversal adding to 180° means the lines are parallel.
Answer: AB || DC

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 1): Find all the other angles inside the following rectangles. (i) Rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O and ∠CAB = 30°. (ii) Rectangle PQRS with diagonals meeting at O and ∠QOR = 110°.
1. (i) OA = OB, because the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so ∠ABD = ∠CAB = 30°.
2. ∠CAD = 90 − 30 = 60, and OA = OD gives ∠ADB = 60.
3. In the same way ∠BDC = 30, ∠ACD = 30 and ∠ACB = 60.
4. At O: ∠AOB = 180 − 60 = 120 and ∠AOD = 180 − 120 = 60.
5. (ii) ∠POS = ∠QOR = 110 (vertically opposite), and ∠QOP = ∠ROS = 180 − 110 = 70.
6. In isosceles ∆QOR the base angles add to 180 − 110 = 70, so ∠OQR = ∠ORQ = 35.
7. ∠OQP = 90 − 35 = 55, and in the same way ∠OPQ = ∠ORS = ∠OSR = 55 and ∠OPS = ∠OSP = 35.
Answer: (i) ∠ABD = 30°, ∠CAD = 60°, ∠ADB = 60°, ∠BDC = 30°, ∠ACD = 30°, ∠ACB = 60°, with 120° and 60° at O; (ii) ∠POS = 110°, ∠QOP = ∠ROS = 70°, ∠OQR = ∠ORQ = 35°, ∠OQP = ∠OPQ = ∠ORS = ∠OSR = 55°, ∠OPS = ∠OSP = 35°

media.title: Quad Dragger
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch. 4 Quadrilaterals (formerly NCERT Ch. 3 Understanding Quadrilaterals), sections on the parallelogram and its special cases. This is the chapter opener and it runs BEFORE any family is named or any property is proved, so nothing here is justified by a criterion the class has not met: the families are held BY CONSTRUCTION and the tool only reports what the construction does and does not fix. The hierarchy is inclusive, as the chapter states it: the rectangle keeps all four of the parallelogram's statements and adds two, which the tool shows as the count 0 subset 4 subset 6.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the drag that breaks or fails to break the property.
whatYouLearned: A property forced by the construction survives every legal position
A property that one drag switches off was only true of the drawn case
Turning a figure never changes a verdict, because every verdict is read from the measures

overview.goal: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A light coordinate grid on a plain working ground, the way a shape is pinned out on squared paper with its corners still free to move. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class looks at one drawn parallelogram, calls it a rectangle because it looks like one, and the figure itself is asked to settle whether those right angles were ever really there.
overview.concept: A figure drawn once can look as though it has properties it does not have. Dragging separates the two: a property forced by the construction survives every legal position, while a property that happened to hold in the drawn case switches off as soon as the figure moves. What survives dragging is what the family really guarantees.
overview.purpose: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into an expandable strip beneath on a 390 px frame. The property panel sits under the readouts. No two vertex handles are ever drawn closer than 60 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the property panel while a prediction is still open, and never render a self crossing or flattened figure. A degenerate figure would give the readouts nothing honest to say.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The construction fixes some relations and leaves the rest free. A relation that the construction fixes cannot fail, because every legal position was built to satisfy it. A relation that the construction leaves free will fail somewhere, and dragging is a search for that somewhere. Failing to break a constructed property is therefore evidence of a very different kind from measuring one figure. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A property that holds in the drawn position is not the same as a property the construction forces. Breaks: A property judged from a single drawn case, so a parallelogram that happens to look like a rectangle is credited with right angles. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Verdicts come from the measures, so turning a figure never changes what it keeps. Breaks: Prototypical images, where a figure is recognised only in its standard orientation and not when it is turned. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Failing to break a property is evidence; the construction that forces it is the reason. Breaks: Treating a run of unbroken drags as a proof, so a property that merely survived is filed as forced. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A refused position protects the readouts; a degenerate figure has nothing honest to report. Breaks: Expecting the tool to draw any four points and grade them, so a degenerate case is read as a bug. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The kept list is a property of the construction, so a figure built with no constraints keeps nothing. Breaks: Reading the property panel as a description of the shape on screen rather than of how it was built.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a constructed parallelogram with the property panel HIDDEN and asks which measurements the class thinks will stay equal under dragging. Beat 2 drags a vertex through several positions while the readouts move and the surviving ticks stay lit. Beat 3 switches to a free quadrilateral where the same statements now flicker off, so the difference between always and this once is visible in one screen. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, moveVertex, showProperties and say. No drag: the agent moves a vertex by named position, never by sweeping.
whatYouLearned: A property forced by the construction survives every legal position
A property that one drag switches off was only true of the drawn case
Turning a figure never changes a verdict, because every verdict is read from the measures
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the constructed parallelogram with the property panel hidden and the readouts on, and ask the class to say out loud which measurements will stay equal when a corner moves. Commit the class list on the prediction pad. Target family parallelogram, the opening four vertices. Never show the property panel before the prediction is committed, and never name a surviving property at this call. Call 2. Move one corner through three separate named positions and let the class watch which ticks hold and which go out. Point at the property panel and then at the kept list. Target family parallelogram, one vertex moved to three positions in turn. Read every side, angle and diagonal number you state from the tool's own readout, never from this plan. Call 3. Switch the family to free with the same list of statements still on screen and point at the statements that go out. Target family free. Say how many statements the kept list still holds, reading the count from the tool's own state and never from memory.

hunts: BREAK IT IF YOU CAN: pick one statement the parallelogram keeps and hunt for a position that switches it off.
TRUE HERE ONLY: find three positions of the parallelogram where an extra tick lights, and say what turns each off.
TILT TEST: drag a rectangle into three unusual orientations and check that not one tick changes.
LOCK ONE SIDE: lock a side length, then find how much of the figure is still free to move.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The construction fixes opposite sides equal, so every legal position was built to satisfy it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The two opposite side readouts move together through every drag and their ticks never go out
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A property the construction forces cannot fail, which is why no drag breaks it

observationsAndConclusions.why: Nothing in the parallelogram construction ties the two diagonal lengths to each other, so they agree only where the figure happens to be a rectangle
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The equal diagonals tick lights in one position and goes out on the very next drag
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: True in the drawn case and guaranteed by the family are two different claims

observationsAndConclusions.why: A free figure is built with no relation fixed, so there is nothing holding any statement in place
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The same list of statements put against a free quadrilateral keeps almost nothing
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The kept list describes how a figure was built, not how it currently looks

media.description: A quadrilateral stands on squared paper with four draggable corners, its equal sides marked with matching hatch strokes, its equal angles with matching arcs and every right angle with the small square the textbook uses. Beside it eight statements each carry a live tick that lights only while the statement holds at the position on screen, and a badge that says whether the CONSTRUCTION keeps it. Dragging is what separates the two: the four statements a parallelogram is built to satisfy never go out however the figure is pulled about, while equal diagonals and four right angles light up in the one position where the parallelogram happens to look like a rectangle and are struck through the moment the next drag lands, labelled with the position number that broke them. The same eight statements are then put to a free quadrilateral, where not one of them survives, so the kept list reads as a fact about how a figure was built rather than about how it currently looks. Side lengths, angles, both diagonal lengths and the two halves at O are all derived from one measure function on the stored vertex coordinates, so no two numbers on the screen can disagree, and near collinear, self crossing, zero length and off paper positions are refused before the drag completes with the reason drawn at the corner that caused it.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a constructed parallelogram with the property panel HIDDEN and asks which measurements the class thinks will stay equal under dragging. Beat 3 switches to a free quadrilateral where the same statements now flicker off, so the difference between always and this once is visible in one screen. scenes.subGoal: Explore the picture with nothing scored and nothing required
scenes.onScreen: The figure, every readout, the property panel, every control, no score and no question. A free quadrilateral on the grid with all readouts on and every vertex draggable.
scenes.animation: Drag update: sides, angles and diagonals recompute in the same frame as the handle moves, so no readout ever lags the figure.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Equal sides are marked with matching ticks and equal angles with matching arcs. A property that survives every drag is written in the kept list, one that does not is left out.
concept.statement: A figure drawn once can look as though it has properties it does not have. Dragging separates the two: a property forced by the construction survives every legal position, while a property that happened to hold in the drawn case switches off as soon as the figure moves. What survives dragging is what the family really guarantees.
prerequisites: the names of the special quadrilaterals
misconceptions: A property judged from a single drawn case, so a parallelogram that happens to look like a rectangle is credited with right angles.
Prototypical images, where a figure is recognised only in its standard orientation and not when it is turned.
concept.why_it_is_true: The construction fixes some relations and leaves the rest free. A relation that the construction fixes cannot fail, because every legal position was built to satisfy it. A relation that the construction leaves free will fail somewhere, and dragging is a search for that somewhere. Failing to break a constructed property is therefore evidence of a very different kind from measuring one figure.
worked_numbers: In a constructed parallelogram the opposite sides stay equal through every drag, and the readouts move together.
In the same parallelogram the diagonals are equal only in the positions where it happens to be a rectangle, and one drag switches that tick off.
In a free quadrilateral even the opposite sides stop being equal, so almost nothing is kept.

extra: A folding clothes rack whose opposite arms stay equal however far it is opened
A criss cross expanding gate that keeps its bars parallel all the way along its track
A hinged pencil box lid that keeps the same width at every opening angle
A photograph of a tilted window frame that still measures as a rectangle
A rubber band stretched over four pegs and then lifted onto one new peg
A cardboard carton flattened and reopened, with its opposite faces still the same size
textbook: The rectangle set out as a list of conditions, so membership is decided by checking rather than by looking
Asking whether opposite sides being parallel and equal is enough on its own to make a quadrilateral a rectangle
Judging the claim that a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square
Reading the angles inside a rectangle from the equal halves its two diagonals cut

lockSideOutcomes.side0: the bottom side is fixed and only the opposite side and the two angles at its ends can still change
lockSideOutcomes.side1: the right hand side is fixed, and the readouts mark which measures are now determined
lockSideOutcomes.side2: the top side is fixed, and because the family already forces opposite sides equal the bottom side is fixed with it
lockSideOutcomes.side3: the left hand side is fixed, leaving the figure one free direction to slide in

setFamilyOutcomes.free: the four corners move independently, and every statement in the panel goes out somewhere, so the kept list empties
setFamilyOutcomes.rectangle: every parallelogram tick stays lit and equal diagonals and four right angles join them, so six statements survive instead of four
setFamilyOutcomes.parallelogram: opposite sides equal, opposite angles equal, next door angles adding to 180 and the diagonals bisecting each other all stay lit through every drag; equal diagonals and right angles flicker

showReadoutsOutcomes.on: the four side lengths, the four angles and both diagonal lengths are on screen and recompute with the figure
showReadoutsOutcomes.off: the measures are hidden and the ticks have to be judged from the marks alone

showPropertiesOutcomes.on: the candidate statements and their live ticks appear beside the figure
showPropertiesOutcomes.off: the panel is hidden, which is the only legal state while a prediction is still open

answer_key.worked: A property that survives every legal drag is guaranteed by the family; one that switches off under dragging was only true of the drawn case.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: which listed properties hold at the current vertices, and which of them are forced by the family rather than incidental.
answer_key.precision: All measures are derived from the stored vertex coordinates. Equality is judged with a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, and the tolerance is stated in the feedback rather than hidden.
answer_key.ground_truth: measures(vertices) = the four side lengths, four angles and two diagonal lengths, computed from the points. holds(property, measures) = the predicate evaluated at the current position. alwaysHolds(family, property) = the family's true property set, held as data and never inferred from the drawn case.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: Near collinear vertices
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked with a minimum separation, and the reason is stated on screen. A flattened quadrilateral has undefined angles, so the tool refuses the position rather than rendering a degenerate figure.

edge_cases.case: A self crossing configuration
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked before the drag completes. Sides may meet only at their endpoints, so a crossing figure is not a quadrilateral and is refused rather than drawn and marked wrong.

edge_cases.case: A zero length side
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked with the reason on screen. Three points and a repeat is a triangle, not a four sided figure.

edge_cases.case: A parallelogram dragged into a rectangle
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The extra ticks light and the tool says they are true here but not kept, because one further drag turns them off. This is the case the whole tool exists for.

edge_cases.case: A figure dragged into an unusual orientation
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Every property is evaluated from the measures, not from the picture, so a tilted rectangle keeps every tick a level one keeps. Orientation never changes a verdict.

startingFamily.description: Which construction the figure opens in: free, parallelogram or rectangle.

constraints: A constructed parallelogram stays a parallelogram no matter how it is dragged. The family is enforced by construction, never by correcting the figure after the fact.
Collinear vertices, self crossing configurations and zero length sides are all blocked before the drag completes, each with its reason on screen.
Vertices are stored as points and every side, angle and diagonal is derived from them, so no two readouts can disagree.
Equality checks use a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, and the tolerance is stated in the feedback.
An answer that a property holds because it looks that way is rejected; the tool asks the student to name the part of the construction that forces it.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

steps: Predict: a constructed parallelogram is drawn with the property panel HIDDEN. The class commits which measurements will stay equal, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Drag: a vertex moves through several positions and the readouts change while the forced ticks stay lit, with the committed guess held beside the kept list.
Free figure: the same statements are put against a free quadrilateral and most of them flicker off, so kept and merely true stand apart.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example moving a vertex to a position a child suggests to test whether a tick survives it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

tool_config.tool_objective: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.

steps: The construction of this figure fixes 4 statements: opposite sides equal, opposite angles equal, next door angles adding to 180 and the diagonals bisecting each other.
Equal diagonals is not one of them, so nothing in the construction holds it.
This position is a rectangle position, where the two lengths happen to agree.
One more drag lengthens one diagonal and the tick goes out.
A statement a drag can switch off is true here and not kept.

The next position tried is not covered by it.
The construction is what settles it: this figure is built with its opposite sides equal.
So the tally is evidence and the construction is the reason.

steps: A flattened figure has a corner with no opening to measure.
An angle readout there would have to report a value it cannot measure.
The property panel reads its ticks from those readouts.
So the figure would be marked from numbers that mean nothing, and the position is refused instead.
items.answer: Because a flattened figure has undefined angles, so every readout and every tick would be meaningless

steps: A free quadrilateral is built from four independent points.
No relation between the sides, the angles or the diagonals is fixed by that.
So every statement can be switched off by some drag.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the property panel while a prediction is still open, and never render a self crossing or flattened figure. A degenerate figure would give the readouts nothing honest to say.
visual_behaviour.scene: A quadrilateral on a light grid with four draggable vertex handles. Equal sides carry matching tick marks and equal angles matching arcs, both in the primary accent. A property panel beside the figure lists candidate statements, each with a tick that lights only while the statement currently holds.
visual_behaviour.layout: Figure fills the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into an expandable strip beneath on a 390 px frame. The property panel sits under the readouts. No two vertex handles are ever drawn closer than 60 px.
readouts: All four side lengths and all four angles, always on screen when readouts are on
How many distinct positions have been tried, and which properties have survived them all
animations: Drag update: sides, angles and diagonals recompute in the same frame as the handle moves, so no readout ever lags the figure.
Tick flicker: a property that stops holding fades its tick over 120 ms rather than snapping, so the student can see the moment it broke.
Kept promotion: a property that survives the tried positions slides from the candidate list into the kept list, which makes surviving a visible event.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: The figure is scaled so the whole quadrilateral fits with every vertex handle at a 44 px hit target; handles are never drawn closer than 60 px apart, and the grid rescales rather than the handles shrinking.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The difference between a property the construction forces and one that merely happens to hold cannot be told from a still picture, so the figure has to be watched moving before the words always and this once carry any meaning

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the difference between the two badges visible before any drag has happened. Four statements read Kept and four read Not true now, on ONE figure, and the class can already see that the panel is answering two different questions: is it true here, and can it ever fail.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one motion. The figure walks three positions; at the middle one the diagonals land on the same number and all four angles land on 90, so two extra ticks light. The next position turns both of them off and the tool strikes them through with the position number that broke them, while the four Kept ticks never so much as flicker. Say that every length on screen changed and the four Kept rows did not.

Beat 3 puts the identical eight statements to a figure built from four independent points. Not one tick is lit and the kept list holds 0. That is the point to name: the panel is a report about the CONSTRUCTION, not a description of the picture.

concepts.concept_name: Rectangles and Squares, Q5

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5): We saw that one of the properties of a rectangle is that its opposite sides are parallel. Can this be chosen as a definition of a rectangle? In other words, is every quadrilateral that has opposite sides parallel and equal, a rectangle?
1. Draw two pairs of parallel lines that do not meet at right angles.
2. They make a quadrilateral with opposite sides parallel and equal, for example with angles 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°.
3. Its angles are not 90°, so it is not a rectangle.
Answer: No; a slanted parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal but is not a rectangle

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 5): If PAIR and RODS are two rectangles, find ∠IOD. (O lies on AI, ∠ORI = 30°, PR = 5 cm and RS = 5 cm.)
1. In ∆ROI, ∠RIO = 90° because PAIR is a rectangle, and ∠ORI = 30°.
2. So ∠ROI = 180 − 90 − 30 = 60.
3. ∠ROD = 90° because RODS is a rectangle.
4. ∠IOD = ∠ROD − ∠ROI = 90 − 60 = 30.
Answer: ∠IOD = 30°

concepts.concept_name: Every square is a rectangle

content.text:
A Special Rectangle: In the quadrilaterals below, are there any non-rectangles?
All these quadrilaterals are rectangles, including (iv). However, it is a special kind of rectangle with all sides of equal length. We know that this quadrilateral is also called a square.
Square: A square is a quadrilateral in which all the angles are equal to 90°, and all the sides are of equal length.
Thus, every square is also a rectangle, but clearly every rectangle is not a square.

In a Venn diagram, a set of objects is represented as points inside a closed curve. Since every square is a rectangle, the oval of squares sits inside the oval of rectangles.

content.text:
If the wooden strips have to be placed such that the thread passing through their endpoints forms a square, what must be done?
What more needs to be done to get equal sidelengths as well? Can this be achieved by properly choosing the angle between the diagonals?
By the SSS condition for congruence, ∆BOA ≅ ∆BOC. These angles are equal and together form a straight angle. So ∠BOA + ∠BOC = 180°. Thus, these angles have to be 90° each.
This shows that the diagonals of a square bisect each other at right angles.
Using this fact, construct a square with a diagonal of length 8 cm.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a square with a diagonal of 8 cm.
1. Draw AC = 8 cm and mark its midpoint O, so OA = OC = 4 cm.
2. Draw the line through O perpendicular to AC.
3. On it mark B and D on opposite sides of O with OB = OD = 4 cm.
4. Join A, B, C and D in order.
5. The diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90°, so ABCD is a square.
Answer: ABCD, with diagonals AC = BD = 8 cm crossing at right angles at their midpoints, is the square

concepts.concept_name: The diagonals of a square bisect its angles

content.text:
Since a square is a special type of rectangle, all the properties of a rectangle hold true for a square.
Property 1: All the sides of a square are equal to each other. Property 2: The opposite sides of a square are parallel to each other. Property 3: The angles of a square are all 90°. Property 4: The diagonals of a square are of equal length and they bisect each other at 90°.
What are the measures of the four angles made by the diagonals at the corners? In ∆ADC, the two angles at A and C together with the right angle at D make 180°. Since AD = DC, the angles at A and C are equal. Thus, each is 45°.
Property 5: The diagonals of a square bisect the angles of the square.

Property 5: The diagonals of a square bisect the angles of the square.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a diagonal cuts a corner of a square into two parts. Are the parts equal?
2. ∆ADC has a right angle at D and two equal sides AD and DC, so its other two angles are equal.
3. Those two angles share 180° − 90° = 90°, so each is 45°.
4. Every corner splits into 45° and 45°: the diagonals bisect the angles of a square.

content.text:
Worked example: In square ABCD the diagonal AC is drawn. Find ∠DAC and ∠DCA.
1. In ∆ADC the angle at D is a right angle, so ∠DAC and ∠DCA share 180 − 90 = 90.
2. AD = DC, so the angles opposite them are equal: ∠DAC = ∠DCA.
3. So each is 90 ÷ 2 = 45.
Answer: ∠DAC = ∠DCA = 45°, so the diagonal bisects the right angles

concepts.concept_name: Practice: find and build squares

content.text:
A square is a rectangle with all sides equal.
Its diagonals are equal and bisect each other at 90°.
Each diagonal bisects the corner angles into 45°.

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 3): Consider a circle with centre O. Line segments PL and AM are two perpendicular diameters of the circle. What is the figure APML? Reason and/or experiment to figure this out.
1. AM and PL are the diagonals of APML.
2. Both are diameters, so they are equal.
3. Both pass through the centre O and OA = OM = OP = OL (radii), so they bisect each other.
4. They are perpendicular, so they meet at 90°.
5. Equal diagonals that bisect each other at 90° make a square.
Answer: APML is a square

Students prove by the SSS condition that the diagonals of a square bisect each other at 90° and construct a square from an 8 cm diagonal.
Students list the properties of a square and show that each diagonal splits a corner of the square into two angles of 45°.
Students recognise squares from their diagonals, construct a square from its diagonal without a protractor, and show that joining the midpoints of a square's sides gives a square.

concepts.concept_name: Kites and Trapeziums, Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 6): Construct a square with diagonal 6 cm without using a protractor.
1. Draw AB = 6 cm.
2. With the compass open more than 3 cm, draw arcs from A and from B on both sides of AB; join the two crossing points. This line is perpendicular to AB through its midpoint O.
3. With the compass set to 3 cm and centre O, mark C and D on this line on opposite sides of AB.
4. Join A, C, B and D in order.
5. The diagonals are 6 cm each, bisect each other and meet at 90°, so ACBD is a square.
Answer: ACBD is the square, with diagonals AB = CD = 6 cm

concepts.concept_name: Kites and Trapeziums, Q7

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 7): CASE is a square. The points U, V, W and X are the midpoints of the sides of the square. What type of quadrilateral is UVWX? Find this by using geometric reasoning, as well as by construction and measurement. Find other ways of constructing a square within a square such that the vertices of the inner square lie on the sides of the outer square.
1. At each corner of CASE the two half sides are equal and the corner angle is 90°.
2. So the four corner triangles are congruent by SAS, and UV = VW = WX = XU.
3. Each corner triangle is isosceles and right-angled, so its base angles are 45° each.
4. On a side, the two 45° angles and the angle of UVWX make a straight angle: 180 − 45 − 45 = 90.
5. UVWX has four equal sides and four right angles, so it is a square.
6. Marking four points the same distance from each corner, all going the same way round, again gives four congruent right triangles and so another square.
Answer: UVWX is a square; any four points at the same distance from the corners, taken the same way round, also make a square

concepts.concept_name: The four angles add up to 360°

content.text:
We have seen that the sum of the angles of a triangle is 180°. There is a similar regularity in the sum of the angles of a quadrilateral.
Consider a quadrilateral SOME. Draw a diagonal SM. We get two triangles ∆SEM and ∆SOM.
In ∆SEM, the three angles add up to 180°. And in ∆SOM, the three angles add up to 180°.
What do we get when we add all six angles? We will have 180° + 180° = 360°.
The sum of all angles in any quadrilateral is 360°.

content.text:
1. Predict first: do the four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, like a triangle, or to something else?
2. Draw the diagonal SM of quadrilateral SOME. It makes two triangles, ∆SEM and ∆SOM.
3. The six angles of the two triangles together make exactly the four angles of SOME.
4. So the four angles add up to 180° + 180° = 360°, for every quadrilateral.

content.text:
Worked example: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 75°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.
1. A diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles, so its angles add up to 180 + 180 = 360.
2. The three known angles add up to 75 + 95 + 110 = 280.
3. The fourth angle is 360 − 280 = 80.
Answer: 80°

concepts.concept_name: Three right angles force the fourth

content.text:
4.2 Angles in a Quadrilateral
Is it possible to construct a quadrilateral with three angles equal to 90° and the fourth angle not equal to 90°?
You might have observed through constructions that this may not be possible. But why not?
This explains why it is impossible for a quadrilateral to have three right angles, with the fourth angle not right angle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can you draw a quadrilateral with three right angles whose fourth angle is not a right angle?
2. The four angles must add up to 360°.
3. Three right angles already use 270°, which leaves exactly 90° for the fourth.
4. So a quadrilateral with three right angles is a rectangle.

content.text:
Worked example: A quadrilateral has three angles of 90°. Find the fourth angle.
1. The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360.
2. The three right angles add up to 90 + 90 + 90 = 270.
3. The fourth angle is 360 − 270 = 90.
Answer: 90°, so the quadrilateral is a rectangle

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 10): Will the sum of the angles in a quadrilateral such as the following one also be 360°? Find the answer using geometric reasoning as well as by constructing this figure and measuring. (ABCD has one corner that caves in.)
1. Draw the diagonal from the caved-in corner to the opposite corner; it lies inside the figure.
2. It splits ABCD into two triangles, each with angles adding up to 180.
3. At the caved-in corner the two triangle angles together make the reflex angle of ABCD.
4. So the four angles of ABCD add up to 180 + 180 = 360.
Answer: Yes; the angle sum is still 360°, using the diagonal that lies inside the figure

media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Understanding Quadrilaterals, the chapter's first general result, read after the student has been dragging figures and now needs something that holds for all of them at once. The class already tore the three corners of a TRIANGLE into a straight line in Class 7, and this tool is built on that memory: four corners make a whole turn, not a straight line. No similarity criterion, no polygon formula and no exterior-angle result is used, because none of them has been met yet; the diagonal and the triangle angle sum are the only facts the argument leans on.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the closed turn or the triangle split that explains it.

overview.goal: The student shows the four angles fit together around a point, and chooses which of the two routes argues for every quadrilateral rather than for this one.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A working sheet with the quadrilateral drawn on one side and a bare meeting point waiting on the other, the way torn paper corners are gathered around a single dot. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class carries the triangle total straight across and says a quadrilateral makes 180 degrees, and four torn corners are asked to settle it.
overview.concept: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees. Tearing the corners and fitting them round a point shows it for the figure in front of you. Cutting the figure with a diagonal into two triangles shows it for every quadrilateral at once, because every quadrilateral splits that way and every triangle has an angle sum of 180.
overview.purpose: The student shows the four angles fit together around a point, and chooses which of the two routes argues for every quadrilateral rather than for this one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure left and meeting point right on a wide frame, figure above and meeting point below on a 390 px frame. The total readout sits beside the meeting point at both widths. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the total while a prediction is still open, and never close the turn automatically. An automatic close would remove the only thing the student is meant to notice.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles whose angles together are exactly the four angles of the original, split between them. Two triangles give 180 plus 180, which is 360. Nothing in that argument depends on which quadrilateral was drawn, which is what makes it a proof rather than a demonstration. The tearing route is convincing but only about the figure that was torn. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

Breaks: Expecting the tool to complete the turn, so the missing corner is never measured. conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with a quadrilateral, its corners untorn and the total HIDDEN, and asks whether the four angles will exactly fill a full turn, leave a gap or overlap. Beat 2 tears the corners and snaps them edge to edge at a point, closing the turn at 360. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with tearCorner, placeCorner, drawDiagonal and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the quadrilateral with all four corners intact and the running total hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether the four corners will fill a full turn, leave a gap or overlap. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the opening four angles. Never tear a corner before the prediction is committed, and never say the total at this call. Call 2. Tear the four corners and place them at the meeting point one at a time, pausing after each so the class can read the running total and the gap still to be filled. Target all four corners placed. Read the running total and the closing total from the tool's own readout, never from this plan. Call 3. Draw the diagonal, name the two triangles it makes, then reshape the original figure and show that the diagonal argument still holds while the torn demonstration would have to be started again. Target the diagonal on, then a reshaped quadrilateral. Say which of the two routes proves it for every quadrilateral, reading the tool's verdict from its own state.

hunts: GAP HUNT: tear three corners only and predict the gap before the readout shows it.
BEND IT IN: drag a corner inward and check the total again with the reflex angle counted.
IMPOSSIBLE SET: type four angles the tool refuses, then say by how much they miss.
RESHAPE AND RETEST: reshape the figure three times and watch which of the two routes has to be redone.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The four interior angles together sweep exactly one full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The four torn corners fit around the meeting point with no gap left and no overlap
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees and not the 180 that triangles give

observationsAndConclusions.why: One diagonal always cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles, and two triangles always give 180 plus 180
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The reshaped figure still closes the turn even though every one of its angles changed
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The diagonal route argues for every quadrilateral, while the tearing route argues only for the figure that was torn

observationsAndConclusions.why: The total is fixed at 360, so any set that misses it cannot belong to a quadrilateral
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A stated set of angles that totals more than 360 leaves the turn overshot and is refused
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Refusing an impossible set is a conclusion about the set, not a failure of the tool

media.description: A lettered quadrilateral A B C D stands on a working sheet with a bare meeting point beside it, and each of its four interior angles is drawn as a coloured wedge of the SAME radius, so the area a corner covers is proportional to its measure. Tapping a corner tears the wedge off, leaving a dashed notch; dragging it to the meeting point snaps it edge to edge against whatever is already there, and a running total climbs while the turn still to be filled is drawn in a second accent until it closes. Concept beat 1 places only TWO wedges, so the Class 7 carry-over answer of 180 degrees arrives on screen as a straight angle with a glaring half-turn gap; beat 2 lands the other two and the readout reaches 360; beat 3 draws the diagonal that actually lies inside the figure, labels both triangles 180 degrees, and shows a DIFFERENT quadrilateral with its corners back on it, so the tearing would have to be redone while the diagonal argument is untouched. A vertex can be dragged in Free Play and the four angles are re-read off the drawn points; a drop that would fold the figure over itself is refused and the corner stays where it was. An angle set that does not total exactly 360, or carries a non positive angle, is refused BEFORE any figure is drawn, and refused with a number: the wedges are laid out anyway and the last one visibly rides over the first, with the overlap measured.

scenes.onScreen: The figure, the meeting point, the total readout, every control, no score and no question. A reshapeable quadrilateral with all corners intact and every control live.

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Angles are marked with arcs at the vertices and keep their measures when torn. A full turn is 360 degrees and is drawn as the complete circle the four corners close.
concept.statement: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees. Tearing the corners and fitting them round a point shows it for the figure in front of you. Cutting the figure with a diagonal into two triangles shows it for every quadrilateral at once, because every quadrilateral splits that way and every triangle has an angle sum of 180.
prerequisites: the angle sum of a triangle is 180 degrees
misconceptions: Angle sum recalled as 180 by carry over from triangles.
A demonstration on one figure taken as a proof for all figures.
concept.why_it_is_true: A diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles whose angles together are exactly the four angles of the original, split between them. Two triangles give 180 plus 180, which is 360. Nothing in that argument depends on which quadrilateral was drawn, which is what makes it a proof rather than a demonstration. The tearing route is convincing but only about the figure that was torn.
worked_numbers: Angles 100, 80, 100 and 80 add to 360 and the torn corners close exactly.
Three angles of 90, 85 and 100 leave a fourth of 85, because the total is fixed.
A set of 90, 90, 90 and 100 sums to 370, so no quadrilateral has those angles.

tearCornerOutcomes.cornerA: the first corner lifts away as a coloured wedge carrying its own measure, and the figure keeps its arc at that vertex
tearCornerOutcomes.cornerB: the second wedge lifts, and the running total on the meeting point climbs by that angle when it is placed
tearCornerOutcomes.cornerC: the third wedge lifts, and the gap readout shows how much of the turn is still open
tearCornerOutcomes.cornerD: the last wedge lifts, and placing it closes the turn exactly and the gap readout falls to zero

chooseRouteOutcomes.tearing: the tool accepts it as a demonstration for this figure and says plainly that it has to be repeated for any other figure
chooseRouteOutcomes.twoTriangles: the tool accepts it as a proof for every quadrilateral, because the argument never used which quadrilateral was drawn

drawDiagonalOutcomes.on: one diagonal is drawn and the figure separates visibly into two triangles, each with its own angle sum shown
drawDiagonalOutcomes.off: the diagonal is removed and the quadrilateral is whole again with its four arcs intact

answer_key.worked: The four angles add to 360 degrees, because a diagonal splits any quadrilateral into two triangles of 180 each.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: the missing fourth angle, or whether a stated set of four angles can belong to a quadrilateral at all.
answer_key.precision: Torn corners are rotated with exact transform matrices so the measured angles do not drift during a drag. Angle sets are validated as exact sums.
answer_key.ground_truth: angleSum(vertices) = the four interior angles, computed from the points, which always total 360. missingAngle(three) = 360 minus their sum. isValidSet(four) = every angle strictly positive and the total exactly 360.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A stated set that does not sum to 360
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Rejected before any figure is drawn, with the shortfall or excess stated. The tool never renders a quadrilateral whose angles could not exist.

edge_cases.case: A non positive angle in a stated set
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Rejected with the reason on screen. A zero or negative angle is not a corner, so there is nothing to tear.

edge_cases.case: A concave quadrilateral
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Still sums to 360 and the tool allows it, with the reflex corner drawn as a reflex arc. Excluding it would suggest the result needs convexity.

edge_cases.case: A corner dragged away and back
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The torn corner keeps its exact measure throughout, so replacing it restores the figure exactly. No measure is recomputed from the dragged position.

edge_cases.case: Three corners placed and one missing
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The gap is shown and measured rather than the turn being closed automatically. An unfinished turn is a legal state and the size of the gap is informative.

showDiagonal.description: Draw the diagonal that splits the figure into two triangles. Off until the second route.

startingAngles.description: The four interior angles the figure opens with, which must total exactly 360.

constraints: Torn corners keep their exact measures during the drag, rotated with exact transform matrices so no angle drifts by a fraction of a degree.
Angle sets that do not total exactly 360, or that contain a non positive angle, are rejected before a figure is drawn.
The turn is never closed automatically. A gap left by a missing corner is drawn and measured, because the gap is the evidence.
The two routes are held as separate arguments with separate state, so the student can compare them rather than seeing them merge.
The original figure can be reshaped at any time and the tool recomputes both routes, so a claim about all quadrilaterals is testable on the spot.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The quadrilateral, the meeting point, the torn corners, the total readout, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the quadrilateral is drawn with its corners untorn and the total HIDDEN. The class commits fill exactly, leave a gap or overlap, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Tear: the four corners come off and snap edge to edge at a common point, closing a full turn, and the readout lands on 360.

play_modes: GAP HUNT: tear three corners only and predict the gap before the readout shows it.
BEND IT IN: drag a corner inward and check the total again with the reflex angle counted.

normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example reshaping the figure to a shape a child suggests and letting the triangle route hold.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish
