visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the total while a prediction is still open, and never close the turn automatically. An automatic close would remove the only thing the student is meant to notice.
visual_behaviour.scene: The quadrilateral with arc marked corners on one side and a meeting point on the other. A torn corner is a coloured wedge carrying its measure. Placed wedges fan out from the meeting point in the primary accent, and the remaining gap is drawn in the second accent until it closes.
visual_behaviour.layout: Figure left and meeting point right on a wide frame, figure above and meeting point below on a 390 px frame. The total readout sits beside the meeting point at both widths.
readouts: The four interior angles, always on screen
The running total of the placed corners, live
The gap still to be filled, whenever the turn is incomplete
animations: Tear: the wedge lifts off the figure over 200 ms leaving a visible notch, so the angle is seen to move rather than to be copied.
Snap: a dragged wedge rotates into contact over 160 ms and the running total ticks, so the turn closes as an accumulating sum.
Diagonal cut: the figure separates into two triangles over 280 ms with the four original angles distributed between them, which is the proof in one gesture.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: The figure and the meeting point are scaled so a wedge stays at least 44 px across at its arc; the panel splits rather than either half shrinking below that.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The corners have to be seen closing a full turn before the diagonal argument is offered, because the tearing is what makes the total believable and the diagonal is then needed only to make it general

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: The four interior angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees
One diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles
Each of those triangles has an angle sum of 180 degrees, and together they carry exactly the four original angles
A set of four angles that does not total 360 degrees belongs to no quadrilateral at all

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the angles out of the question text and set them, rejecting any set that does not total exactly 360 or that contains a non positive value. If the question gives three angles, compute the fourth and build the figure from all four. The figure drawn must carry every angle the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.
question_integration.learn_source: props.learnQuestions (delivery_mode = 'Learn'). Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.
scene_fields: showDiagonal, on when the question is about the triangle route
tornCorners, when the question freezes a part torn state
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no angles in it ('why is the triangle route stronger than the tearing route?') has nothing to tear. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool one figure torn and closed beside the same figure reshaped and split by a diagonal, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.
question_integration.practice_source: props.questions (delivery_mode = 'Practice'), drawn at random by the platform inside the difficulty and subtype targets. Mandatory checkpoints are never served here.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the wrong rule FAIL on screen rather than to warn against it. Two wedges are placed, the readout says 180 degrees and the meeting point is a bare half circle with an obvious half-turn gap. A class that has carried the triangle total across sees its own answer drawn, and sees it half finished, before anyone says it is wrong.
Beat 2 is the payoff and it is a picture, not a statement: the other two wedges land, the gap closes to nothing and nothing rides over. Read the total off the tool, never from this plan.

Beat 3 is where the two routes separate. The figure on screen is a DIFFERENT quadrilateral with its corners back on it, so the torn demonstration would have to be started again, while the diagonal still cuts two triangles and still gives 180 plus 180. Say which route survived the change; that difference is the whole lesson.
media.generation_prompt: Angle Sum Folder: four corners torn off a quadrilateral and dragged to a common point where they close a full turn, with a second route that cuts the figure into two triangles
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the four angles and say whether they will fill a turn, leave a gap or overlap. 2. Tap a corner to tear it off. 3. Drag the torn corner to the meeting point and read the running total. 4. Repeat until all four corners are placed and the gap closes. 5. Draw a diagonal and name the two triangles it makes. 6. Reshape the original quadrilateral and see which route still works without being redone. 7. Choose the route that proves it for every quadrilateral and say why. 8. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: How can three angles of a quadrilateral give the fourth?
media.context: Quadrilaterals. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Three angles of a four sided shape are seventy five, ninety five and one hundred ten degrees. The video cuts the shape into two triangles to get the total of the four angles, and Keeko then doubts and says the fourth angle is ninety degrees.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a diagonal cuts a four sided shape into two triangles, so its four angles add to three hundred sixty degrees. Watch for students who guess ninety for the fourth angle because rectangles have right angles.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

items: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 75°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.

source: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 75°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.
video_script.why: The child sees why the four angles of any quadrilateral add to three hundred sixty degrees, and uses the total to find the fourth angle when three are known.
video_script.substitution: Cut the shape into two triangles with a diagonal, add the angles of the two triangles, and take the three known angles away from the total.
video_script.anchor: a four sided shape with a diagonal, three angles marked 75, 95 and 110 degrees and the fourth angle unknown

final_answer.spoken: the fourth angle is eighty degrees

maths_rules: a diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles, each with angle sum 180 degrees
the angles of the two triangles together make the four angles of the quadrilateral, so the total is 180 + 180 = 360 degrees
the fourth angle is 360 - 280 = 80 degrees

media.title: Do the angles of a caved-in four sided shape add to 360 degrees?
media.context: Quadrilaterals. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A four sided shape has one corner that caves in, and the video asks if its four angles still add to three hundred sixty degrees. It joins the caved-in corner to the opposite corner, splits the shape into two triangles, and checks by drawing and measuring.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the diagonal from the caved-in corner lies inside the shape, so it makes two triangles whose angles fill the four angles of the shape. Watch for students who think the rule fails because one angle is bigger than a straight angle.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

video_script.substitution: Join the caved-in corner to the opposite corner so the diagonal lies inside, add the angles of the two triangles, and match them with the four angles of the shape.
video_script.anchor: quadrilateral ABCD whose corner D caves in, with the diagonal DB drawn inside it
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, the angles of eigh B C D still add to three hundred sixty degrees

final_answer.value: Yes, the angle sum is still 360°
final_answer.spoken: yes, the angles of eigh B C D still add to three hundred sixty degrees

maths_rules: in ABCD the corner D caves in, so the diagonal DB lies inside the shape
DB splits ABCD into triangles ABD and CBD, each with angle sum 180 degrees
the angle of ABCD at D is angle ADB + angle BDC, and the angle at B is angle ABD + angle DBC
the angles at A and C belong to one triangle each
the six angles of the two triangles are exactly the four angles of ABCD, so the total is 180 + 180 = 360 degrees
check: draw such a shape, measure the four angles with a protractor and add them to get about 360
video_script.design: One idea: the diagonal from the caved-in corner lies inside, so two triangles fill the four angles and the total stays 360 degrees. The caved-in shape with its diagonal stays on the board.

concepts.concept_name: Parallel opposite sides that are not a rectangle

content.text:
4.3 More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides
Rectangles (and therefore squares) have parallel opposite sides. Are there quadrilaterals that have parallel opposite sides that are not rectangles?
This can be easily done by drawing two pairs of parallel lines, ensuring that they do not meet at right angles.
Thus, a larger set of quadrilaterals exists in which the opposite sides are parallel. Such quadrilaterals are called parallelograms.
Is a rectangle a parallelogram? A rectangle has opposite sides parallel. So, it satisfies the parallelogram's definition. Hence, it is indeed a parallelogram.
Let us represent this relation using a Venn diagram.
Draw a parallelogram with adjacent sides of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm, and an angle of 30° between them.
Step 1: Draw line segments AB = 4 cm and AD = 5 cm with an angle of 30° between them. Step 2: Draw a line parallel to AB through the point D, and a line parallel to AD through B. Mark the point at which these lines intersect as C.

Worked example: Construct a parallelogram ABCD with AB = 4 cm, AD = 5 cm and an angle of 30° between them.
1. Draw AB = 4 cm.
2. At A draw a 30° angle and mark D on its arm with AD = 5 cm.
3. Through D draw a line parallel to AB; through B draw a line parallel to AD.
4. Mark the point where these two lines meet as C.
5. ABCD has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so it is a parallelogram.
Answer: ABCD is the required parallelogram, and it is not a rectangle

concepts.concept_name: The angles of a parallelogram

content.text:
Deduction 6: What can we say about the angles of a parallelogram?
In the parallelogram ABCD, AB||CD, and AD is a transversal to them. ∠A + ∠D = 180° (sum of the internal angles on the same side of a transversal). Therefore, ∠D = 180° − 30° = 150°.
Using these equations, we get ∠B = 150° and ∠C = 30°.
We see that in this parallelogram, the adjacent pairs of angles add up to 180° and opposite pairs of angles are equal.
What about the opposite angles? Will they be equal in all parallelograms? If yes, how can we be sure? Let us take one of the angles to be x.
Since ∠P + ∠R = 180°, ∠R = 180 − x. Similarly, ∠A = 180 − (180 − x) = x.
Therefore, this shows that the opposite angles of a parallelogram are always equal.

content.text:
1. Predict first: one angle of a parallelogram is 30°. Are the other angles 30° too?
2. Next-door angles sit between a pair of parallel sides, on the same side of a transversal, so they add up to 180°.
3. So the neighbours of 30° are 150°, and the angle opposite 30° is 180° − 150° = 30°.
4. With one angle x: its neighbours are 180° − x, and the opposite angle is 180° − (180° − x) = x. Opposite angles are always equal.

content.text:
Worked example: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 30°. Find ∠B, ∠C and ∠D.
1. AB || CD with transversal AD, so ∠A + ∠D = 180.
2. So ∠D = 180 − 30 = 150.
3. AD || BC with transversal AB, so ∠A + ∠B = 180, and ∠B = 150.
4. ∠C + ∠D = 180, so ∠C = 180 − 150 = 30.
Answer: ∠B = 150°, ∠C = 30°, ∠D = 150°

concepts.concept_name: The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal

content.text:
Deduction 7: What can we say about the sides of a parallelogram?
By looking at a parallelogram, it appears that the opposite sides are equal. Can we again use congruence to show this? Which two triangles can be considered for this?
In ∆ABD and ∆CDB, the angles marked with a single arc are equal as they are the opposite angles of a parallelogram. Since AD||BC, and BD is a transversal to it, the angles marked with double arcs are equal as they are alternate angles.
So, by the AAS condition, the triangles are congruent, that is, ∆ABD ≅ ∆CDB. Therefore, AD = CB, and AB = CD.
Is it wrong to write ∆ABD ≅ ∆CBD? Why?
Property 1: The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. Property 2: The opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel. Property 3: In a parallelogram, the adjacent angles add up to 180°, and the opposite angles are equal.

2. Draw the diagonal BD. In ∆ABD and ∆CDB: ∠A = ∠C (opposite angles), ∠ADB = ∠CBD (alternate angles), and BD is shared.
3. AAS makes them congruent, so AD = CB and AB = CD.
4. Match the letters: A goes with C. Writing ∆CBD would pair AB with CB, which are not equal sides.

content.text:
Worked example: In parallelogram ABCD, AB = 4 cm and AD = 5 cm. Find CB and CD, and say why ∆ABD ≅ ∆CBD is wrong.
1. Join the diagonal BD.
2. ∠BAD = ∠DCB, because they are opposite angles of the parallelogram.
3. AD || BC with transversal BD, so ∠ADB = ∠CBD (alternate angles).
4. BD is common, so by AAS ∆ABD ≅ ∆CDB.
5. So CB = AD = 5 cm and CD = AB = 4 cm.
6. ∆CBD would match A with C but B with B, claiming AB equals CB, yet AB is 4 cm and CB is 5 cm.
Answer: CB = 5 cm and CD = 4 cm; ∆ABD ≅ ∆CBD is wrong because its vertices do not match

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 9): What type of a quadrilateral is one in which the opposite sides are equal? Justify your answer. (Hint: Draw a diagonal and check for congruent triangles.)
1. Let ABCD have AB = CD and AD = CB, and draw the diagonal BD.
2. ∆ABD ≅ ∆CDB by SSS, because BD is common.
3. So ∠ABD = ∠CDB; these are alternate angles for AB and DC with transversal BD, so AB || DC.
4. Also ∠ADB = ∠CBD, so AD || BC.
5. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
Answer: A parallelogram

media.title: Sides And Angles Lab
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash chapter 4 Quadrilaterals (old NCERT chapter 3, Understanding Quadrilaterals). The class has met transversals, co-interior angles, supplementary angles, congruence by SSS and SAS, and the 360° angle sum of a quadrilateral. This mount sits at the Distinguish beat: the parallelogram's angle relations are separated from each other, because one drawn case cannot settle which pair is equal and which pair adds to 180. Classification is INCLUSIVE here, exactly as the book has it, a square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and a parallelogram is also a trapezium, so no preset ever clears a row an earlier family had.

finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the marked figure that explains it.
whatYouLearned: In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and next door angles add to 180 degrees
A rectangle adds right angles to a parallelogram and a rhombus adds equal sides
The families differ by the relations they force, not by how they happen to look

overview.goal: The student states which sides and angles are equal or supplementary in each named family, and writes the minimum set of properties that pins a family down.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A single quadrilateral on a plain ground with a family selector above it and a property checklist standing beside it, the way one figure is marked up in a notebook margin. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says that next door angles in a parallelogram must be equal because the opposite ones are, and a slow sweep of the whole shape is asked to settle which pair is which.
overview.concept: Each family fixes a particular pattern of equal and supplementary relations. In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. Adding one more condition moves you to a rectangle or a rhombus, and adding both gives a square, so the families differ by which relations they force and not by how they happen to look.

overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with the checklist to the right on a wide frame and beneath on a 390 px frame. The family selector sits above the figure at both widths and the sweep control below it. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not fill a checklist row before its prediction is committed, and never mark a relation the family does not force. A mark the family cannot guarantee is a false property claim.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

titleFraming.normal: Free Play · Sides And Angles Lab

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. In a parallelogram a pair of adjacent angles sits between the same two parallel sides, so they are co-interior and add to 180. The opposite angles are then each 180 minus the same value, so they are equal to each other. The colour coding and the linking arcs make those two different relations visually different, which is exactly where the confusion lives. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A relation that holds at one point of the sweep is a position, not a property of the family. Breaks: A property judged from the drawn case, so a parallelogram in a rectangle position is credited with right angles. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Reaching a special position does not add a property to the family that was swept. Breaks: Reading a coincidence at one parameter value as a new guaranteed property. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Equal and supplementary are different relations that coincide only at 90 degrees. Breaks: Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A mark is a claim the family forces, so an unmarked pair is a pair nothing guarantees. Breaks: Expecting every quadrilateral to carry the parallelogram marks, so a trapezium is read as one. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A proposed property set is refuted by one figure that satisfies it and sits outside the family. Breaks: Believing a set of properties that every member has is automatically enough to define the family.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a parallelogram with the checklist HIDDEN and asks whether next door angles will add to 180 or be equal. Beat 2 sweeps the shape parameter while the equal sides hold their matching colours and the linking arcs on adjacent angles stay at 180. Beat 3 switches preset to a rectangle, where the same arcs now also read 90 each, so what the family adds is visible as a change in the marks. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, sweep, revealRow and say. No drag: the agent sets the parameter by value, never by sweeping continuously.

The families differ by the relations they force, not by how they happen to look
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the parallelogram with the equal sides coloured, no arcs drawn and the checklist hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether next door angles add to 180 or are equal. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target family parallelogram at the opening parameter. Never draw an arc or reveal a checklist row before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Sweep the shape parameter slowly from one end of its range to the other and point at the linking arc as it holds while the angles themselves keep changing. Target family parallelogram, a sweep across the full parameter range. Read the two angle values and the linking arc total from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Change the family preset to rectangle with the same arcs still drawn, and ask the class what the extra condition bought. Target family rectangle. Say what the equal pair and the supplementary pair each now read, taking both numbers from the tool's own state.

hunts: NEVER FLICKERS: sweep a parallelogram from end to end and list every mark that never goes out.
POSITION HUNT: find the parameter value where a rhombus shows right angles, then sweep past it.

FAMILY LADDER: switch from parallelogram to rectangle to square and name what each step bought.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Ninety and ninety are equal to each other and also add to 180, so the two relations agree at that one value
observationsAndConclusions.observe: At the rectangle preset the equal pair and the supplementary pair give the same number
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Agreement in one family is not sameness, which is why a rectangle is the worst figure to learn the difference from

media.description: One lettered quadrilateral stands on a plain ground with a property checklist beside it. Equal sides carry matching hatch ticks and a shared colour, equal angles carry same-radius arcs, the parallel pairs carry arrowhead chevrons, and every angle pair the family forces to add to 180 is joined by a linking arc that prints the SUM rather than the word supplementary. A shape parameter sweeps the figure inside its family, and the marks the family forces never flicker while a relation that merely happens to hold at one value is drawn dashed and captioned 'at this value only', so a coincidence can be watched switching off. Switching the family preset from parallelogram to rectangle, rhombus or square ADDS one condition at a time and the checklist grows without ever resetting, which is how the inclusive classification is read off the list rather than off the outline. Free Play lets the student predict each checklist row before opening it and then test a proposed minimum property set, which the tool answers by drawing a figure that satisfies the set and sits outside the family. Practice serves a session drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, each item rendering the figure its own question describes, with the asked measure masked until the answer is in.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the family and the measures from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the colour coding, the checklist and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a parallelogram with the checklist HIDDEN and asks whether next door angles will add to 180 or be equal. Beat 2 sweeps the shape parameter while the equal sides hold their matching colours and the linking arcs on adjacent angles stay at 180. Beat 3 switches preset to a rectangle, where the same arcs now also read 90 each, so what the family adds is visible as a change in the marks. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, sweep, revealRow and say. No drag: the agent sets the parameter by value, never by sweeping continuously.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own figure. Give a missing side or angle in a named family, say which pairs are equal and which are supplementary, or write the minimum property set. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the marked figure that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student chooses any family preset, sweeps the shape parameter through its range, and reveals any checklist row after predicting it. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

whatYouLearned: In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and next door angles add to 180 degrees
A rectangle adds right angles to a parallelogram and a rhombus adds equal sides
The families differ by the relations they force, not by how they happen to look

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. concept.notation: Equal sides are drawn in matching colours, equal angles carry matching arcs, and a supplementary pair is joined by a single linking arc labelled 180.
concept.statement: Each family fixes a particular pattern of equal and supplementary relations. In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. Adding one more condition moves you to a rectangle or a rhombus, and adding both gives a square, so the families differ by which relations they force and not by how they happen to look.
prerequisites: the angle sum of a quadrilateral
misconceptions: Opposite angles confused with adjacent ones, so the pair that is equal and the pair that is supplementary are swapped.
Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal.
concept.why_it_is_true: In a parallelogram a pair of adjacent angles sits between the same two parallel sides, so they are co-interior and add to 180. The opposite angles are then each 180 minus the same value, so they are equal to each other. The colour coding and the linking arcs make those two different relations visually different, which is exactly where the confusion lives.
worked_numbers: In a parallelogram with one angle of 70, the adjacent angle is 110 and the opposite angle is 70 again.
In a rectangle every one of those values is 90, so equal and supplementary agree by coincidence.
In a rhombus of side 6 all four sides share one colour, while the angles still split into two equal pairs.

revealRowOutcomes.allAnglesRight: ticks only for rectangle and square, which is the condition that separates them from the rhombus
revealRowOutcomes.oppositeSidesEqual: ticks for parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle and square, and stays empty for a general trapezium
revealRowOutcomes.oppositeAnglesEqual: ticks for every parallelogram family and stays empty for a general trapezium
revealRowOutcomes.adjacentAnglesSupplementary: ticks for every parallelogram family, and the linking arc prints 180 beside it

setFamilyOutcomes.square: one side colour and one angle arc value, because both extra conditions are in force at once
setFamilyOutcomes.rhombus: all four sides share one colour while the angles still split into two equal pairs
setFamilyOutcomes.rectangle: every angle arc reads 90, so the equal pair and the supplementary pair give the same number
setFamilyOutcomes.trapezium: only one pair of sides is parallel, so the opposite angles row never ticks and only one linking arc survives
setFamilyOutcomes.parallelogram: two side colours, two angle arc pairs and a linking arc reading 180 on each adjacent pair

answer_key.worked: In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles add to 180, and the same two relations survive the whole sweep.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: the missing side or angle in the named family, or which pairs the marks currently join.
answer_key.precision: Presets are defined by construction rules rather than fixed coordinates, so every measure is derived and the family cannot be left by sweeping. Equality uses a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units.
answer_key.ground_truth: measures(family, parameter) = the sides, angles and diagonals produced by the construction. equalPairs(measures) and supplementaryPairs(measures) = the pairs the marks join, evaluated live. minimalSet(family) = the smallest condition set whose figures are exactly that family.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A parallelogram swept into a rectangle position
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The extra equalities light and the tool says they are true at this parameter value but not part of the family. Sweeping on turns them off again.

edge_cases.case: A rhombus swept into a square position
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Every side keeps one colour and the angles all reach 90 at once. The tool names the position rather than the family, so the coincidence is not mistaken for a property.

edge_cases.case: A trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Only the co-interior pairs on the legs carry linking arcs. The tool never marks a relation that the family does not force.

edge_cases.case: A proposed minimal set that is too weak
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool generates a figure that satisfies the set but is outside the family and asks whether it belongs, so the set is tested rather than marked.

edge_cases.case: The end of a parameter sweep
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The sweep stops before the figure degenerates, with the reason on screen, because a flattened figure has no angles to mark.

shapeParameter.description: Where the sweep starts within the family's legal range, as a percentage.

startingFamily.description: The family preset the lab opens on.

constraints: The family constraint holds throughout the sweep. Presets are defined by construction rules and not by fixed coordinates, so sweeping cannot leave the family.
A checklist row fills only after the student has predicted it, so the tool never answers a question before it has been asked.
Equal sides are coloured and supplementary pairs are arced by two visually distinct devices, because the confusion the tool targets is between those two relations.
A relation that holds only at the current parameter value is named as a position and not as a property, and sweeping on turns it off.
The sweep stops before the figure degenerates, with the reason on screen, rather than rendering a flattened shape.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The figure with its colour coding and arcs, the family selector, the property checklist, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: a parallelogram is drawn with the checklist HIDDEN. The class commits add to 180 or equal for next door angles, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Sweep: the shape parameter moves and the equal sides keep their colours while the linking arcs on adjacent angles hold at 180 throughout.
Change family: the preset moves to a rectangle and the same arcs now read 90 each, so what the extra condition added is visible in the marks.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and two families have been marked side by side. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: A parallelogram with equal sides coloured, no arcs drawn and the checklist hidden, the predict pad open on 'In a parallelogram, will next door angles add to 180 or be equal?'.

play_modes: NEVER FLICKERS: sweep a parallelogram from end to end and list every mark that never goes out.
POSITION HUNT: find the parameter value where a rhombus shows right angles, then sweep past it.
TOO WEAK: propose a property set, look at the figure the tool draws, and say what is missing.
FAMILY LADDER: switch from parallelogram to rectangle to square and name what each step bought.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting a parameter value a child names to test whether a relation survives it.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.

a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. steps: The parallelogram construction forces 3 relations: the opposite sides are equal; the opposite angles are equal; next door angles add to 180.
Equal angles all round is not one of them.
This is one value of the sweep, where the figure sits in a rectangle position.
Sweeping on turns both of the new marks off again.
So they name a position and not a property of the family.
items.answer: No: they hold at this parameter value only, and sweeping on turns them off

steps: A rhombus forces 4 relations, including all four sides equal.
All four angles equal is not among them.
At this parameter value the angles happen to arrive at 90 together.
Sweeping on moves them apart again while the side colours stay put.
So the tool names the position and leaves the family list alone.
items.answer: The position: the sides stay equal for the family, and the right angles belong to this value of the sweep
items.method: Decide what a rhombus in a square position has gained

steps: Next door angles in any parallelogram add to 180.
In a rectangle each of them measures 90.
180 minus 90 is 90, so the supplement of one is the other.
The two relations agree here because 90 is its own supplement.
Sweep to a parallelogram with an angle of 70 and one reads 70 while the other reads 110.
items.answer: No: they agree only because 90 is its own supplement, and they part company as soon as the angle moves
items.method: Distinguish equal from supplementary where the two happen to agree
items.question: In a rectangle two next door angles are both equal and add to 180. Does that make equal and supplementary the same relation?

stickers.type_method: Distinguish equal from supplementary where the two happen to agree

items.checkpoint: Equal and supplementary are different relations that coincide only at 90 degrees.
items.misconception: Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal.

steps: A linking arc marks a pair the family forces to add to 180.
Only the two legs run between the single pair of parallel sides.
So only the angle pairs on those legs are co-interior.
The remaining pairs are not forced by anything, so marking them would claim a property the family does not give.
The trapezium therefore forces 0 of the listed relations.
items.answer: Only the pairs on the two legs, because a mark the family cannot guarantee would be a false claim
items.method: Predict which marks a trapezium carries
items.question: A trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides is loaded. Which angle pairs carry a linking arc, and why not the others?

items.checkpoint: A mark is a claim the family forces, so an unmarked pair is a pair nothing guarantees.
items.misconception: Expecting every quadrilateral to carry the parallelogram marks, so a trapezium is read as one.

steps: The proposed set is a claim that nothing outside the family can satisfy it.
The tool builds a figure that satisfies the set.
That figure has one pair of equal sides and no parallel pair at all.
It is outside the family, so the proposed set is too weak.
A set is minimum only when nothing outside the family can meet it.
items.answer: That the set is too weak, because a figure outside the family satisfies it
items.method: Test a proposed minimum property set against a figure outside the family
items.question: A student proposes that one pair of equal opposite sides is enough to make a parallelogram. The tool draws a figure satisfying that and asks whether it belongs. What has that shown?

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the two relations side by side on one figure, because the misconception is that there is only one. The linking arc prints 70° + 110° = 180° while the two opposite arcs both read 70°: the class can see that the pair that is EQUAL and the pair that ADDS TO 180 are different pairs, and that they are marked with different devices for exactly that reason.

Beat 2 is the justification, and it needs motion. The figure is swept from one end of its range to the other; every number on screen changes and the same two marks hold throughout, because a pair of next-door angles sits between the same two parallel sides and is therefore co-interior. What survives the sweep is what the family guarantees, that is the whole argument and it cannot be made from a still frame.

Beat 3 adds one condition. The preset moves to a rectangle and the checklist GROWS: the three parallelogram rows stay ticked and a fourth lights. That is the inclusive hierarchy read off the list, and it is also where equal and supplementary agree, each next-door angle reads 90 and 90 is its own supplement, which is precisely why a rectangle is the worst figure to learn the difference from.

media.instructions_for_student: Read the marks. Sides that carry the same hatch ticks are equal, angles that carry the same arcs are equal, and two angles joined by a linking arc add to the number printed on it. Drag the shape value to sweep the figure inside its family, and watch which marks never go out, those are the ones the family forces. A mark drawn with a dashed line is true only at the value you are looking at, and sweeping on turns it off. In Free Play, say Yes or No to a row before you open it, then test your own set of properties and see whether the tool can draw a figure that fits it and still sits outside the family.

1. Predict first: are the diagonals of a parallelogram equal? Do they cross at their midpoints?
2. In the 4 cm by 5 cm parallelogram the diagonals clearly differ in length, so they need not be equal.

4. The diagonals bisect each other. They meet at no fixed angle: it changes from one parallelogram to another.

content.text:
Worked example: In parallelogram EASY the diagonals AY and ES meet at O, with AY = 10 cm and ES = 6 cm. Find OA, OY, OE and OS, and say why ∆AOE ≅ ∆SOY is wrong.
1. AE = YS, because they are opposite sides of the parallelogram.
2. AE || YS, so ∠OAE = ∠OYS and ∠OEA = ∠OSY (alternate angles).
3. By ASA, ∆AOE ≅ ∆YOS, so OA = OY and OE = OS.
4. OA = OY = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm and OE = OS = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
5. ∆SOY would pair A with S and E with Y, but A matches Y and E matches S.
Answer: OA = OY = 5 cm and OE = OS = 3 cm; ∆SOY is in the wrong order

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms and rhombuses, question 2): Using the diagonal properties, construct a parallelogram whose diagonals are of lengths 7 cm and 5 cm, and intersect at an angle of 140°.
1. Draw AC = 7 cm and mark its midpoint O, so OA = OC = 3.5 cm.
2. At O draw a line making 140° with OC.
3. On it mark B and D on opposite sides of O with OB = OD = 2.5 cm, so BD = 5 cm.
4. Join A, B, C and D in order.
5. The diagonals bisect each other, so ABCD is a parallelogram.
Answer: ABCD, with diagonals 7 cm and 5 cm bisecting each other at 140°, is the parallelogram

concepts.concept_name: Equal sides without right angles

content.text:
4.4 Quadrilaterals with Equal Sidelengths
Are squares the only quadrilaterals that have equal sidelengths? Let us explore this question through construction.
Draw two equal sides AD and AB, that are not perpendicular to each other. Can we complete this quadrilateral so that all its sides are of the same length?
Mark a point C whose distance from B and D is equal to AB (or AD). To do this, measure AB using a compass. Keeping this length as the radius, cut arcs from B and D.
Note that we could have constructed such a quadrilateral by taking any angle less than 180° (in place of 50°).
A quadrilateral in which all the sides have the same length is a rhombus.

1. Predict first: is a square the only quadrilateral with four equal sides?
2. Draw AB = AD with an angle of 50° between them, not 90°.
3. With the compass set to AB, cut arcs from B and from D. They cross at C, and all four sides are equal.
4. A quadrilateral with all sides equal is a rhombus; any angle below 180° works in place of 50°.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a quadrilateral ABCD with all sides 5 cm and ∠A = 50°.
1. Draw AB = 5 cm.
2. At A draw a 50° angle and mark D on its arm with AD = 5 cm.
3. With the compass set to 5 cm, draw an arc from B and an arc from D.
4. Mark the point where the arcs cross as C, and join BC and DC.
5. AB = BC = CD = DA = 5 cm, so ABCD is a rhombus.
Answer: ABCD is a rhombus with a 50° angle, and it is not a square

concepts.concept_name: Every rhombus is a parallelogram

content.text:
Deduction 9: What can we say about the angles in a rhombus?
Consider a rhombus GAME. In ∆GAE, since GE = GA, a = d. Similarly, in ∆MAE, since ME = MA, b = c. It can be seen that ∆GAE ≅ ∆MAE (How?). So, a = b, c = d and ∠G = ∠M.
Thus, we have, a = b = c = d.
In ∆ADB, we have a + a + 50 = 180°. So, a = 65°. Thus, the angles of the rhombus ABCD are 50°, 130°, 50°, and 130°.
Consider the lines EM and GA and its transversal AE. Since the alternate angles are equal, EM||GA. Similarly, GE||AM.
As opposite sides are parallel, GAME is also a parallelogram. Thus, every rhombus is a parallelogram, and the properties of a parallelogram hold true for a rhombus as well.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in the rhombus with a 50° angle, what are the other three angles?
2. Diagonal AE of rhombus GAME makes two isosceles triangles, and ∆GAE ≅ ∆MAE by SSS, so all four angles it makes are equal.
3. Those equal angles are alternate angles, so EM || GA and GE || AM: every rhombus is a parallelogram.
4. In the 50° rhombus, each angle made by the diagonal is half of 180° − 50°, which is 65°, so the rhombus has angles 50°, 130°, 50° and 130°.

content.text:
Worked example: Rhombus ABCD has ∠A = 50°. Find its other angles.
1. Diagonal BD makes four equal angles a: two at B and two at D.
2. In ∆ADB, a + a + 50 = 180, so the two angles a add up to 180 − 50 = 130.

concepts.concept_name: The diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles

content.text:
So a rhombus is a parallelogram, and a rectangle is also a parallelogram. How can this be represented using a Venn diagram? Where will the set of squares occur in this diagram?
We know that a square is a rectangle. Since the opposite sides of a square are parallel, a square is also a parallelogram. Further, since all the sides of a square have the same length, a square is also a rhombus.
Property 1: All the sides of a rhombus are equal to each other. Property 2: The opposite sides of a rhombus are parallel to each other. Property 3: In a rhombus, the adjacent angles add up to 180°, and the opposite angles are equal. Property 4: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other. Property 5: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles.
Are the diagonals of a rhombus equal?
Deduction 10: In the rhombus GAME, we have ∆GEO ≅ ∆MEO (why?). So, ∠GOE = ∠MOE. As they add up to 180°, they should be 90° each.
Property 6: Diagonals of a rhombus intersect each other at an angle of 90°.

content.text:
Worked example: In rhombus GAME the diagonals meet at O, with GM = 8 cm and EA = 6 cm. Find the angle at O, GO and EO.
1. A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each other: GO = MO and EO = AO.
2. In ∆GEO and ∆MEO: GE = ME, GO = MO, and EO is common, so ∆GEO ≅ ∆MEO by SSS.
3. So ∠GOE = ∠MOE, and together they make 180, so each is 90.
4. GO = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm and EO = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
Answer: The diagonals meet at 90°; GO = 4 cm and EO = 3 cm

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms and rhombuses, question 1): Find the remaining angles in the following quadrilaterals. (i) Parallelogram PEAR with ∠P = 40°. (ii) Parallelogram PQRS with ∠P = 110°. (iii) Rhombus UVWX with diagonal XV and ∠XVU = 30°. (iv) Rhombus OIEA with diagonal OE and ∠OEA = 20°.
1. (i) Adjacent angles add up to 180, so ∠E = ∠R = 180 − 40 = 140, and ∠A = ∠P = 40.
2. (ii) ∠Q = ∠S = 180 − 110 = 70, and ∠R = ∠P = 110.
3. (iii) The diagonal XV bisects ∠V and ∠X, so ∠V = 30 + 30 = 60 and ∠X = 60.
4. Then ∠U = ∠W = 180 − 60 = 120.
5. (iv) The diagonal OE bisects ∠E and ∠O, so ∠E = 20 + 20 = 40 and ∠O = 40.
6. Then ∠A = ∠I = 180 − 40 = 140.
Answer: (i) ∠E = 140°, ∠A = 40°, ∠R = 140°; (ii) ∠Q = 70°, ∠R = 110°, ∠S = 70°; (iii) ∠V = ∠X = 60°, ∠U = ∠W = 120°; (iv) ∠E = ∠O = 40°, ∠A = ∠I = 140°

tool_config.title: Rhombus Hinge
tool_config.idea: Four equal rods hinged at the corners make a rhombus that changes shape as the hinge opens, but opposite angles stay equal, neighbouring angles stay at 180°, and the diagonals always bisect each other at 90° and bisect the corners. Only at 90° do the diagonals become equal, and the rhombus becomes a square.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students construct a quadrilateral with four equal sides and a 50° angle and define a rhombus.
Students show that a diagonal of a rhombus makes four equal angles, use this to find the angles of the 50° rhombus, and deduce that every rhombus is a parallelogram.
Students place rhombuses, rectangles and squares in one Venn diagram, list the properties of a rhombus, and prove by the SSS condition that its diagonals meet at 90°.
Students find the remaining angles of parallelograms and rhombuses and construct a rhombus from its diagonals.

concepts.concept_name: Parallelograms and Rhombuses, Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms and rhombuses, question 3): Using the diagonal properties, construct a rhombus whose diagonals are of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm.
1. Draw AC = 5 cm and mark its midpoint O.
2. Draw the line through O perpendicular to AC.
3. On it mark B and D on opposite sides of O with OB = OD = 2 cm, so BD = 4 cm.
4. Join A, B, C and D in order.
5. The diagonals bisect each other at 90°, so all four sides are equal and ABCD is a rhombus.
Answer: ABCD, with diagonals 5 cm and 4 cm bisecting each other at right angles, is the rhombus

concepts.concept_name: Quadrilaterals on a geoboard

content.text:
4.5 Playing with Quadrilaterals
Geoboard Activity: Take a geoboard and some rubber bands. If you do not have these, you could just use the dot grid papers given at the end of the book for this activity.
Place two rubber bands perpendicular to each other, forming diagonals of equal length. Join the ends. What is the quadrilateral that you get? Justify your answer.
Extend one of the diagonals on both sides by 2 cm. What quadrilateral will you get now? Justify your answer.

content.text:
1. Predict first: two equal rubber bands cross at right angles at their midpoints. What shape do their ends make?
2. The diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90°, so the shape is a square.
3. Now stretch one band 2 cm further at each end. Its midpoint stays at the crossing point.
4. The diagonals still bisect each other at 90° but are no longer equal: the shape is a rhombus, not a square.

content.text:
Worked example: Two rubber bands of 4 cm cross at right angles at their midpoints. Name the quadrilateral their ends make, and name it again after one band is extended by 2 cm at each end.
1. The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so the quadrilateral is a rectangle.
2. They also meet at 90°, so all four sides are equal: it is a square.
3. The extended band is now 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 cm long and still has its midpoint at the crossing.
4. The diagonals still bisect each other at 90°, so all four sides are equal, but the diagonals are 4 cm and 8 cm, so it is not a rectangle.
Answer: First a square; after extending one diagonal, a rhombus

Joining Triangles

content.text:
1. Predict first: two identical triangles are placed side by side along a common side. Which quadrilaterals can you get?
2. Two equilateral triangles of 8 cm give four sides of 8 cm: a rhombus.
3. Two 8, 8, 6 triangles joined along the 6 cm side give four sides of 8 cm: again a rhombus.
4. Joined along an 8 cm side, one copy turned half round gives a parallelogram with sides 8, 6, 8, 6; one copy flipped over gives a kite with sides 8, 8, 6, 6.

content.text:
Worked example: Join two copies of the triangle with sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 6 cm in different ways and name the quadrilaterals.
1. Along the 6 cm side: the four outer sides are all 8 cm, so the quadrilateral is a rhombus.
2. Along an 8 cm side, with one copy turned half round: the outer sides are 8, 6, 8 and 6 cm, opposite sides are equal, so it is a parallelogram.
3. Along an 8 cm side, with one copy flipped over: two neighbouring sides are 8 cm and the other two are 6 cm, so it is a kite.
4. Two equilateral triangles of 8 cm, joined in the same way, give four sides of 8 cm: a rhombus.
Answer: A rhombus, a parallelogram and a kite; two equilateral triangles give a rhombus

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many different quadrilaterals can two copies of a 6, 9, 12 triangle make?
2. There are three sides to join along, and two ways to join along each: turned half round or flipped over.
3. Turned half round always gives a parallelogram: 9, 12, 9, 12 or 6, 12, 6, 12 or 6, 9, 6, 9.
4. Flipped over always gives two pairs of equal neighbouring sides, a kite. Only the kite flipped over the 12 cm side is the usual shape; the other two cave in at one corner.

content.text:
Worked example: Two copies of a triangle with sides 6 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm are joined along a side. List the quadrilaterals you can get.
1. Along the 6 cm side, turned half round: sides 9, 12, 9 and 12, a parallelogram.
2. Along the 9 cm side, turned half round: sides 6, 12, 6 and 12, a parallelogram.
3. Along the 12 cm side, turned half round: sides 6, 9, 6 and 9, a parallelogram.
4. Flipped over the 12 cm side: sides 6, 6, 9 and 9 with equal neighbours, a kite.
5. Flipped over the 6 cm or the 9 cm side: again two pairs of equal neighbouring sides, a kite, but one that caves in at a corner.
Answer: Three parallelograms and three kites; only the kite on the 12 cm side has no corner that caves in

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 1): Find all the sides and the angles of the quadrilateral obtained by joining two equilateral triangles with sides 4 cm.
1. Each side of the quadrilateral is a side of an equilateral triangle, so all four sides are 4 cm.
2. Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60.
3. The two corners not on the joined side are single triangle angles: 60 each.
4. The two corners on the joined side are made of two triangle angles: 60 + 60 = 120 each.
5. Check: 60 + 120 + 60 + 120 = 360.
Answer: All sides are 4 cm; the angles are 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°, a rhombus

media.title: Diagonal Lab
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 4 'Quadrilaterals'. The chapter builds quadrilaterals FROM their diagonals (construct a rhombus from its two diagonals; join the ends of two perpendicular diameters and name the figure), so dragging the diagonals and letting the outline follow IS the textbook activity, done without a compass. The student already knows each family's diagonal properties and the hierarchy square inside rectangle inside parallelogram; this tool runs that reading BACKWARDS. Vertices are capital letters in order (ABCD), the diagonals are AC and BD and the crossing is O, exactly as the book prints them. Pythagoras is available from Class 7 and is said out loud rather than assumed. The word 'diamond' never appears.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct family set, and the revealed outline that explains it.
whatYouLearned: Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram
Equal diagonals add the rectangle condition and a right angled crossing adds the rhombus condition
A condition set can name a set of families, because a square is a rectangle and a rhombus at once

overview.goal: The student identifies a quadrilateral family from its diagonal behaviour alone, and sets the diagonals to produce a stated target family.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: Two crossing segments alone on a plain ground with no figure drawn around them, the way two rubber bands are stretched across a pegboard. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is told only that the two diagonals are equal and cut each other in half, and is asked to name the shape before anything is drawn.
overview.concept: The diagonals decide the family. Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. Add equal lengths and it is a rectangle; add a right angle crossing instead and it is a rhombus; add both and it is a square. Because a square is a rectangle, a condition set can name more than one family at once, so the answer is a set.
overview.purpose: The student identifies a quadrilateral family from its diagonal behaviour alone, and sets the diagonals to produce a stated target family.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Diagonals fill the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and beneath on a 390 px frame. Every endpoint keeps a 44 px hit target and no two are drawn closer than 60 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal the outline while a prediction is still open, and never report a single family name where the conditions allow more than one. A single name would teach that equal diagonals force a square.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The outline is always the quadrilateral formed by joining the four diagonal endpoints in order, so the diagonals fully determine it. Bisecting makes the two halves of each diagonal equal, which forces the opposite sides to match. Equal lengths then force equal diagonals in the outline, and a right angled crossing forces equal sides. Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, which is why they compose. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

Answer: Because the families nest, so conditions that guarantee one family guarantee every wider one too

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A condition set names a family, and the family named here contains the square rather than being it. Breaks: Equal diagonals assumed to force a square, ignoring every non square rectangle. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A failed family test is reported as a named missing condition, not as no answer. Breaks: Diagonals treated as decoration, so a figure whose diagonals fail a condition is thought to have no family at all. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Diagonal conditions guarantee a whole chain of families, so the honest answer is a set. Breaks: Believing each condition set picks out exactly one shape name. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The crossing point is defined by both diagonals, so it cannot be moved off either of them. Breaks: Treating the crossing point as a free handle rather than as the meeting the conditions are measured from. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The outline exists only because the four endpoints are not all on one line. Breaks: Forgetting that the outline is built from the diagonals, so a degenerate crossing is expected to draw something.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with two diagonals that are equal and bisect each other, the outline HIDDEN, and asks what shape this must be. Beat 2 reveals the outline as a rectangle and the three readouts are read back as the reason. Beat 3 adds the right angle lock, the outline becomes a square, and the tool says that the earlier answer was a set and not a single shape. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setDiagonals, toggleRightAngle, revealOutline and say. No drag: the agent sets endpoints by position, never by sweeping.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on two equal diagonals bisecting each other with the outline hidden and all three condition readouts on, and ask the class to name the family out loud. Commit the class name on the prediction pad. Target the two equal diagonals with the crossing at both midpoints. Never reveal the outline before the prediction is committed, and never name the family at this call. Call 2. Reveal the outline and read the three conditions back one at a time as the reason it had to come out that way. Target the outline on. Read both diagonal lengths and the crossing angle from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Switch the right angle lock on with the same two diagonals in place, and let the outline change. Target the right angle lock on. Say which families the tool now lists in the family set readout, taking the list from the tool's own state and never from memory.

hunts: BUILD THE FAMILY: set the diagonals so the outline is a rhombus that is not a square, then say which condition you left out.
ONE CONDITION AT A TIME: start from a general crossing and turn on one condition at a time, naming what each buys.
NOT A SQUARE: make equal bisecting diagonals give three different rectangles, none of them square.
MISSING PIECE: aim at a target family, get it wrong on purpose, and read which condition the tool names.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The four diagonal endpoints joined in order are the whole figure, so the diagonals determine the outline completely
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The outline is drawn only after the three condition readouts have been read, and it is exactly what they promised
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The diagonals are a defining condition, not a feature to be read off the shape afterwards

observationsAndConclusions.why: Equal lengths and bisection together force the rectangle conditions and nothing further
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Equal diagonals that bisect each other give many different rectangles and only a few of them are squares
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Equal diagonals never force a square, because every rectangle that is not a square has them too

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, so the conditions compose instead of replacing each other
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Switching the right angle lock on turns the same crossing into a square
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A condition set can name more than one family, which is why the honest answer is sometimes a set of names

media.description: Two crossing segments stand alone on a plain working ground with no figure drawn around them: the diagonals AC and BD, meeting at O. Tick marks carry the bisection (one tick on each half of AC, two on each half of BD, drawn only where that diagonal really is cut in half), a small square at O carries the right-angled crossing, and both lengths and the crossing angle are printed live along the top of the scene. Three labelled booleans - bisect each other, equal in length, meet at right angles - sit beside the figure, and beneath it the tool prints the whole SET of families the current conditions guarantee rather than a single name, so a square is reported as sitting inside the rectangle set and the rhombus set at once. The outline is never drawn independently: it is the quadrilateral A B C D formed by joining the four endpoints in order, and it appears as a consequence of the conditions rather than as a separate piece of evidence. In Free Play the student drags any endpoint, slides the crossing along a diagonal, locks the crossing at 90 degrees and sets a target family, and the tool answers a failed target by NAMING the condition that is still missing. Two positions are refused with the reason on screen - a crossing that is not on both diagonals, and two diagonals dragged towards one straight line - because neither describes a figure that exists.

concept.notation: The three diagonal conditions are written as bisect each other, equal in length and meet at right angles. A family answer may be a set of names, not a single name.
concept.statement: The diagonals decide the family. Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. Add equal lengths and it is a rectangle; add a right angle crossing instead and it is a rhombus; add both and it is a square. Because a square is a rectangle, a condition set can name more than one family at once, so the answer is a set.
prerequisites: the diagonal properties of the special quadrilaterals
misconceptions: Diagonals treated as decoration rather than as a defining condition, so they are read off a shape and never used to make one.
Equal diagonals assumed to force a square, ignoring every non square rectangle.
concept.why_it_is_true: The outline is always the quadrilateral formed by joining the four diagonal endpoints in order, so the diagonals fully determine it. Bisecting makes the two halves of each diagonal equal, which forces the opposite sides to match. Equal lengths then force equal diagonals in the outline, and a right angled crossing forces equal sides. Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, which is why they compose.
worked_numbers: Diagonals of 10 and 10 bisecting each other give a rectangle, and only some of those are squares.
Diagonals of 10 and 6 bisecting at right angles give a rhombus that is not a square.
Diagonals of 8 and 8 bisecting at right angles give a square, which is in both of the earlier sets.

answer_key.worked: Diagonals that are equal and bisect each other name the rectangle family, which includes the square, so the answer is a set and not one shape.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn diagonals: the three boolean conditions, the family set they imply, and whether a target family has been produced.
answer_key.precision: Every condition is measured from the endpoint coordinates with a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback. The ground truth is a set of family names, never a single name.
answer_key.ground_truth: bisect(d1, d2) = the crossing point is the midpoint of both. equal(d1, d2) = the two lengths agree within tolerance. perpendicular(d1, d2) = the crossing angle is 90 within tolerance. familySet(conditions) = every family name consistent with them, so a square condition set returns square inside rectangle and rhombus.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class commits a name with the outline NOT yet drawn. The three booleans are the only evidence on screen, which is the whole point: the diagonals have to become a defining condition rather than a feature read off a finished shape. Ask for the name out loud before moving on, and do not say the word square.

Beat 2 is the payoff and it is a consequence, not a new fact. The four endpoints join in order and a rectangle appears, so read the three conditions back one at a time as the reason it had to come out that way. The same 16 and 16 that were on screen a moment ago are still on screen.

Beat 3 adds ONE condition and the earlier answer is seen to have been a set all along. The crossing locks at 90 degrees, the outline becomes a square, and rectangle stays lit beside it. If rectangle went dark the tool would be teaching that a square is not a rectangle, which is the misconception the beat exists to break.

content.text:
4.6 Kite and Trapezium
One of the ways the two triangles of sides 6 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm can be joined together is as follows. This quadrilateral looks like a kite. Observe that the adjacent sides are of the same length.
Kite: A kite is a quadrilateral that can be labelled ABCD such that AB = BC, and CD = DA.
Property 1: In the kite, show that the diagonal BD (i) bisects ∠ABC and ∠ADC, (ii) bisects the diagonal AC, that is, AO = OC, and is perpendicular to it.
Hint: Is ∆AOB ≅ ∆COB?

content.text:
Worked example: ABCD is a kite with AB = BC and CD = DA, and its diagonals meet at O. Show that BD bisects ∠ABC and that BD is perpendicular to AC with AO = OC.
1. In ∆ABD and ∆CBD: AB = CB, AD = CD, and BD is common, so ∆ABD ≅ ∆CBD by SSS.
2. So ∠ABD = ∠CBD: BD bisects ∠ABC (and likewise ∠ADC).
3. In ∆AOB and ∆COB: AB = CB, ∠ABO = ∠CBO, and BO is common, so ∆AOB ≅ ∆COB by SAS.
4. So AO = OC, and ∠AOB = ∠COB.
5. These two angles make a straight angle of 180, so each is 180 ÷ 2 = 90.
Answer: BD bisects ∠ABC and ∠ADC, and it cuts AC in half at right angles

concepts.concept_name: Practice: construct a kite from its diagonals

content.text:
A kite has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides.
One diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other.
The other diagonal need not be bisected.

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 2): Construct a kite whose diagonals are of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm.
1. Draw AC = 6 cm and draw its perpendicular bisector, meeting AC at O.
2. On the bisector mark B 2 cm from O on one side and D 6 cm from O on the other side, so BD = 2 + 6 = 8 cm.
3. Join A, B, C and D in order.
4. B and D lie on the perpendicular bisector of AC, so BA = BC and DA = DC: ABCD is a kite.
5. Splitting 8 cm as 4 cm and 4 cm would give a rhombus, which is a special kite.
Answer: ABCD with AC = 6 cm, BD = 8 cm, BD the perpendicular bisector of AC and O not the midpoint of BD

concepts.concept_name: Trapeziums and their angles

content.text:
Trapezium: Parallelograms are quadrilaterals that have parallel opposite sides. We get a new type of quadrilateral if we relax this condition.
Trapezium: A trapezium is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel opposite sides.
Construct a trapezium. Measure the base angles (marked in the figure). Can you find the remaining angles without measuring them?
Since PQ||SR, we have Property 1: ∠S + ∠P = 180° and ∠R + ∠Q = 180°.
Using these facts, the remaining angles can easily be found. Verify your answer after finding them.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a trapezium has base angles 70° and 55°. Can you find the top angles without measuring?
2. A trapezium needs at least one pair of parallel opposite sides, so a parallelogram is a trapezium too.
3. With PQ || SR, each slanting side is a transversal, so the two angles along it add up to 180°.
4. So ∠S = 180° − ∠P and ∠R = 180° − ∠Q.

content.text:
Worked example: Trapezium PQRS has PQ || SR, ∠P = 70° and ∠Q = 55°. Find ∠S and ∠R.
1. PS is a transversal to the parallel lines PQ and SR, so ∠S + ∠P = 180.
2. So ∠S = 180 − 70 = 110.
3. QR is a transversal too, so ∠R = 180 − 55 = 125.
4. Check: 70 + 55 + 125 + 110 = 360.
Answer: ∠S = 110° and ∠R = 125°

concepts.concept_name: The isosceles trapezium

content.text:
When the non-parallel sides of a trapezium have the same lengths, the trapezium is called an isosceles trapezium.
Construct an isosceles trapezium UVWX, with UV||XW. Measure ∠U. Can you find the remaining angles without measuring them?
Consider line segments XY and WZ perpendicular to UV. What type of quadrilateral is XWZY?
Since XW||UV, a = 180° − ∠XYZ = 90°, and b = 180° − ∠WZY = 90°. Hence, XWZY is a rectangle.
Now, it can be shown that ∆UXY ≅ ∆VWZ. (How?) Thus, ∠U = ∠V.
Property 2: In an isosceles trapezium, the angles opposite to the equal sides are equal.

Since XW||UV, a = 180° − ∠XYZ = 90°, and b = 180° − ∠WZY = 90°. Hence, XWZY is a rectangle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in a trapezium whose slanting sides are equal, are the two base angles equal?
2. Drop XY and WZ perpendicular to UV. XWZY has four right angles, so it is a rectangle and XY = WZ.
3. ∆UXY and ∆VWZ are right triangles with UX = VW and XY = WZ, so they are congruent by RHS.
4. So ∠U = ∠V, and each top angle is 180° minus the base angle below it.

content.text:
Worked example: UVWX is an isosceles trapezium with UV || XW, UX = VW and ∠U = 65°. Find ∠V, ∠W and ∠X.
1. Draw XY and WZ perpendicular to UV; XWZY is a rectangle, so XY = WZ.
2. ∆UXY and ∆VWZ have right angles at Y and Z, UX = VW and XY = WZ, so ∆UXY ≅ ∆VWZ by RHS.
3. So ∠V = ∠U = 65.
4. UX is a transversal to the parallel sides, so ∠X = 180 − 65 = 115, and likewise ∠W = 115.
Answer: ∠V = 65°, ∠W = 115°, ∠X = 115°

concepts.concept_name: Practice: angles of trapeziums

content.text:
A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel opposite sides.
The two angles along each slanting side add up to 180°.
In an isosceles trapezium the base angles are equal.
content.publication_text:

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 3): Find the remaining angles in the following trapeziums. (i) A trapezium with angles 105° and 135° at the ends of one parallel side. (ii) An isosceles trapezium with an angle of 100°.
1. (i) Each slanting side is a transversal to the parallel sides, so its two angles add up to 180.
2. The remaining angles are 180 − 105 = 75 and 180 − 135 = 45.
3. (ii) The slanting sides are equal, so the angles at the ends of the same parallel side are equal: the other one next to 100 is also 100.
4. The angles below them are 180 − 100 = 80 each.
Answer: (i) 75° and 45°; (ii) 100°, 80° and 80°

content.text:
Parallelogram, Kite, Trapezium, Rectangle, Square, Rhombus.

content.text:
Worked example: Give every family name that belongs to a square.
1. All its angles are 90°, so it is a rectangle.
2. All its sides are equal, so it is a rhombus.
3. Its opposite sides are parallel, so it is a parallelogram, and so also a trapezium.
4. Its neighbouring sides are equal in two pairs, so it is a kite.
Answer: A square is a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram, a trapezium and a kite

content.text:
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.
A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus. (State whether this is true or false.)

content.text:
1. Predict first: the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other at right angles. Must it be a rhombus?
2. The four triangles at the crossing have two equal half-diagonals and a right angle between them.
3. SAS makes them congruent, so all four sides are equal: a rhombus.
4. But perpendicular diagonals alone are not enough: a kite has them and is not always a rhombus.

content.text:
Worked example: The diagonals AC and BD of ABCD bisect each other at O at right angles. Show that ABCD is a rhombus.
1. OA = OC and OB = OD, because the diagonals bisect each other.
2. The four angles at O are each 90.
3. In ∆AOB and ∆COB: OA = OC, ∠AOB = ∠COB, and OB is common, so they are congruent by SAS and AB = CB.
4. In the same way BC = CD and CD = DA.
5. All four sides are equal, so ABCD is a rhombus.
Answer: ABCD is a rhombus

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 4): Draw a Venn diagram showing the set of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles, and squares. Then, answer the following questions. (i) What is the quadrilateral that is both a kite and a parallelogram? (ii) Can there be a quadrilateral that is both a kite and a rectangle? (iii) Is every kite a rhombus? If not, what is the correct relationship between these two types of quadrilaterals?
1. Draw parallelograms holding rectangles and rhombuses, with squares in their overlap; draw kites overlapping parallelograms exactly in the rhombuses.
2. (i) A parallelogram has opposite sides equal; a kite has neighbouring sides equal in pairs, so all four sides are equal: a rhombus (squares included).
3. (ii) A kite that is a rectangle has equal neighbouring sides and opposite sides equal, so all sides are equal and all angles 90°: a square.
4. (iii) No. A kite can have sides 6, 6, 9 and 9, which is not a rhombus. Every rhombus is a kite.
Answer: (i) A rhombus; (ii) Yes, a square; (iii) No; every rhombus is a kite, but not every kite is a rhombus
