(i) What is the quadrilateral that is both a kite and a parallelogram? (ii) Can there be a quadrilateral that is both a kite and a rectangle? (iii) Is every kite a rhombus? If not, what is the correct relationship between these two types of quadrilaterals?
steps: Draw parallelograms holding rectangles and rhombuses, with squares in their overlap; draw kites overlapping parallelograms exactly in the rhombuses.
(i) A parallelogram has opposite sides equal; a kite has neighbouring sides equal in pairs, so all four sides are equal: a rhombus (squares included).
(ii) A kite that is a rectangle has equal neighbouring sides and opposite sides equal, so all sides are equal and all angles 90°: a square.
(iii) No. A kite can have sides 6, 6, 9 and 9, which is not a rhombus. Every rhombus is a kite.
content.answer: (i) A rhombus; (ii) Yes, a square; (iii) No; every rhombus is a kite, but not every kite is a rhombus

overview.goal: The student places each figure in every region it belongs to, including nested ones, and states what a card must satisfy to move inward.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: Nested rings drawn on a plain ground with a tray of figure cards beneath them, the way sorted cards are laid out inside chalked circles on the floor. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class refuses to put the square card inside the rectangle ring, and the card's own measured properties are asked to settle where it goes.
overview.concept: The families nest because each inner one satisfies every condition of the ones around it plus at least one more. A square meets the rectangle conditions and the rhombus conditions, so it sits in both and therefore in the parallelogram ring and the quadrilateral ring too. Membership is decided by measured properties, not by the name a figure is usually given.
overview.purpose: The student places each figure in every region it belongs to, including nested ones, and states what a card must satisfy to move inward.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Rings fill the main panel with the tray directly beneath. On a 390 px frame the rings shrink to keep every label and the overlap legible and the tray scrolls horizontally. Every card keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not pre-place any card while a prediction is still open, and never let the square rest outside the overlap. A square filed as its own separate shape is the misconception drawn.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Membership is a set of conditions, and adding conditions can only shrink the set of figures that satisfy them. So the family with more conditions sits inside the family with fewer. A square has every rectangle condition, so it cannot fail to be in the rectangle ring, whatever it is usually called. The rings are a picture of that containment and not a filing system for names. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A figure belongs to every region whose conditions it meets, and the overlap is the only honest place for the square. Breaks: Reading a rejected placement as an opinion of the tool rather than as a failed measurement. Breaks: Reading the diagram as a filing system for shape names rather than as containment of condition sets.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the nested rings EMPTY and asks where a square belongs on the diagram. Beat 2 sorts the obvious cards, each landing in its outermost failing region so the nesting becomes visible. Beat 3 places the square in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses and refuses every other position, so inclusion is enforced rather than argued. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, showProperties, rotateCard and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its region.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the empty nested rings with every card face up in the tray, and ask the class to say out loud where the square card belongs. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the empty rings and the full tray. Never place a card before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Place the straightforward cards one at a time into their innermost regions and let the rings fill from the outside in, opening each card as it lands so the class hears the properties that decided it. Targets the parallelogram card, the rectangle card and the rhombus card. Read the region counts from the tool's own readout, never from this plan. Call 3. Take the square card and try it in each outer region in turn, letting the tool refuse every placement except the innermost overlap and name the ring it would have to leave each time. Target the square card into the overlap of the rectangle and rhombus rings. Say how many regions the square finally lights, reading the number from the tool's own state.

hunts: DEEPEST CARD: find the card that reaches the innermost region and say which conditions carried it there.
SPIN TEST: rotate three cards through odd angles and check that not one of them changes region.
BUILD TO ORDER: construct a figure that lands in exactly three regions.
BOUNCE HUNT: get each card bounced once on purpose and collect the property named each time.

media.description: Nested rings sit on a plain working ground - Quadrilaterals holding Parallelograms, and inside that two overlapping lobes, Rectangles and Rhombuses, whose lens-shaped overlap is drawn as its own region and labelled Squares. A tray of figure cards waits beneath. Every card is a real quadrilateral held as four vertices, so its sides, angles and diagonals are MEASURED rather than looked up by name, and the rings a card belongs to are derived from those measures alone. Dragging a card onto a ring is a claim of membership: the tool locks it in when the claim is exactly right, accepts it as true but incomplete when the card could go further in, and bounces it back naming the condition it failed and printing the measured value that decided it - 23.1 degrees between the pairs that should have been parallel, or an angle of 72 degrees where 90 was asked for. The square card is therefore refused everywhere except the lens, because resting in the rectangles lobe outside it would record the card as not a rhombus. Tapping a card opens its measured properties grouped by the ring each one decides; turning a card recomputes those properties and moves it not one ring; and the student can build a figure of their own on a snapped 0-20 grid and watch the same conditions decide where it belongs. Region counts stay on screen throughout, so containment is a number the class can read and not only a picture.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the nested rings EMPTY and asks where a square belongs on the diagram. Beat 2 sorts the obvious cards, each landing in its outermost failing region so the nesting becomes visible. Beat 3 places the square in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses and refuses every other position, so inclusion is enforced rather than argued. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, showProperties, rotateCard and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its region.

concept.notation: Nested rings are drawn from the outside in: quadrilaterals, then parallelograms, then rectangles and rhombuses, overlapping at squares. Being in an inner region means being in every ring around it.
concept.statement: The families nest because each inner one satisfies every condition of the ones around it plus at least one more. A square meets the rectangle conditions and the rhombus conditions, so it sits in both and therefore in the parallelogram ring and the quadrilateral ring too. Membership is decided by measured properties, not by the name a figure is usually given.
prerequisites: the defining conditions of each family
misconceptions: Class inclusion refused, so a square is not counted as a rectangle.
Naming by appearance, so a figure in an unusual orientation is placed in the wrong region.
concept.why_it_is_true: Membership is a set of conditions, and adding conditions can only shrink the set of figures that satisfy them. So the family with more conditions sits inside the family with fewer. A square has every rectangle condition, so it cannot fail to be in the rectangle ring, whatever it is usually called. The rings are a picture of that containment and not a filing system for names.
worked_numbers: A square of side 5 belongs to squares, rectangles, rhombuses, parallelograms and quadrilaterals, five regions at once.
A rectangle of 8 by 3 belongs to rectangles, parallelograms and quadrilaterals but not to rhombuses.
A rhombus of side 6 with a 70 degree angle belongs to rhombuses, parallelograms and quadrilaterals but not to rectangles.

extra: Every rickshaw is a vehicle, and not every vehicle is a rickshaw
Every mango is a fruit, so the mango basket sits inside the fruit basket
Every member of the cricket team is also a student of the school
A tile that is a floor tile and also a square tile, and is filed under both
Every one rupee coin is money, and not all money is a coin
A stamp album where the local stamps sit inside the country page
Every teacher in the staff room is also a member of the school
A shop list where wheat sits inside grains and grains sit inside food
Every bus on this route is a bus, and not every bus is on this route
textbook: Drawing the nested picture of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles and squares

answer_key.worked: A square belongs in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses, and therefore also in parallelograms and quadrilaterals. Inner membership implies every outer one.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the measured figure: the full set of regions each card belongs to, evaluated from its properties rather than from its name.
answer_key.precision: Membership is a set of boolean predicates evaluated on the figure's measures, so an unusual orientation is handled automatically. Equality uses a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback.
answer_key.ground_truth: properties(vertices) = the measured side, angle and diagonal predicates. regions(properties) = every ring whose conditions all hold. A correct placement is the innermost region, and membership of every outer ring follows from it.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: The square card
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: It rests only in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses and every other placement is refused. The refusal names the region the square would have to leave, which is the inclusion argument in one move.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Placed by its measured properties, so a tilted rectangle lands exactly where an upright one does. Orientation never changes membership.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Bounced back with the failed property named and measured, so the reason is the figure and not the label.

constraints: Membership is modelled as a set of boolean predicates evaluated on the figure's measures, then region fit is derived, so unusual orientations are handled without special cases.
Region containment is enforced: a placement in an inner region also counts as membership of every outer region, and the tool never records one without the others.

The predicate set is shared with the definition checker and the claim judge, so the three tools cannot disagree about the same figure.
Equality checks use a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback whenever it decides a placement.

a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not pre-place any card while a prediction is still open, and never let the square rest outside the overlap. A square filed as its own separate shape is the misconception drawn.
visual_behaviour.scene: Nested rings on a plain ground, labelled from the outside in, with the innermost overlap of rectangles and rhombuses drawn as its own region. Figure cards sit in a tray beneath, each showing its outline; a placed card locks flat inside its region and an opened card shows its measured properties.
visual_behaviour.layout: Rings fill the main panel with the tray directly beneath. On a 390 px frame the rings shrink to keep every label and the overlap legible and the tray scrolls horizontally. Every card keeps a 44 px hit target.
readouts: How many cards sit in each region, always on screen
How many cards are still in the tray, live
For the opened card: its measured properties grouped by the ring each decides
animations: Card lock: a correct placement settles over 160 ms and every outer ring it now belongs to pulses in turn, so inclusion is shown as a chain rather than a point.
Card bounce: a wrong placement travels back to the tray over 220 ms and flips to show the failed property on arrival, so the explanation lands where the card does.
Rotation: the card turns while its property list stays completely still, which is the answer to naming by appearance in one image.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Ring radius is derived from the panel width so the innermost overlap stays at least 80 px across and every label sits clear of the rings; cards never shrink below a 44 px hit target and the tray scrolls instead.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The rings have to be filled from the outside in before the word nested is used, so that containment is watched happening rather than accepted as a diagram to be copied

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: A family with more conditions sits inside a family with fewer, because adding a condition can only shrink the set of figures that satisfy it
A square satisfies every rectangle condition and every rhombus condition, so it sits in the overlap of the two
Every rectangle, every rhombus and every square is a parallelogram, and every one of them is a quadrilateral
Membership is decided by the measured properties of a figure, never by the name it is usually given or the way it happens to be turned

question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the reading method public before the argument starts. The rings are empty, every card is face up in the tray, and the rhombus card is open so the class watches HOW a card is read - four sides of 6, angles of 72 and 108, three rings lit. Ask where the square belongs OUT LOUD before beat 2; the tool never renders that ask.

Beat 2 is the containment seen rather than stated. Five cards land in their innermost rings and the counts fill from the outside in: Quadrilaterals 5, Parallelograms 3, Rectangles 1, Rhombuses 1. Every card that reached an inner ring was counted in every ring around it, which is the whole of nesting in four numbers.

Beat 3 settles the argument the chapter exists for. The square card is refused by the rectangles lobe with 'it would have to leave Rhombuses' and the measured row 7, 7, 7, 7 printed beside it, then rests in the lens and lights five regions at once while the rectangle card next to it reads three. The number is the argument; do not paraphrase it into a caption.

concepts.concept_name: Kites and Trapeziums, Q8

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 8): If a quadrilateral has four equal sides and one angle of 90°, will it be a square? Find the answer using geometric reasoning as well as by construction and measurement.
1. Four equal sides make it a rhombus, so it is a parallelogram.
2. Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180, so the neighbours of 90 are 180 − 90 = 90.
3. The opposite angle equals 90 too, so all four angles are 90.
4. Four equal sides and four right angles make a square.
Answer: Yes, it is a square

content.text:
Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 11): State whether the following statements are true or false. Justify your answers. (i) A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square. (ii) A quadrilateral having three right angles must be a rectangle. (iii) A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other must be a parallelogram. (iv) A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus. (v) A quadrilateral in which the opposite angles are equal must be a parallelogram. (vi) A quadrilateral in which all the angles are equal is a rectangle. (vii) Isosceles trapeziums are parallelograms.
1. (i) False: such diagonals give a rectangle, which need not be a square.
2. (ii) True: the fourth angle is 360 − 270 = 90.
3. (iii) True: the triangles at the crossing are congruent in opposite pairs, giving equal alternate angles, so opposite sides are parallel.
4. (iv) False: a kite has perpendicular diagonals but need not be a rhombus.
5. (v) True: with angles x, y, x, y we get 2x + 2y = 360, so neighbouring angles add up to 180 and opposite sides are parallel.
6. (vi) True: each angle is 360 ÷ 4 = 90.
7. (vii) False: its slanting sides are not parallel, unless it is a rectangle.
Answer: (i) False (ii) True (iii) True (iv) False (v) True (vi) True (vii) False

concepts.concept_name: What we found about quadrilaterals

content.text:
A rectangle is a quadrilateral in which the angles are all 90°. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal and parallel; its diagonals are of equal length and they bisect each other.
A square is a quadrilateral in which all the angles are 90°, and all the sides are of equal length. The diagonals of a square are of equal lengths, bisect each other at 90° and bisect its angles.
A parallelogram is a quadrilateral in which opposite sides are parallel. Its opposite sides are equal, adjacent angles add up to 180°, opposite angles are equal, and its diagonals bisect each other.
A rhombus is a quadrilateral in which all the sides have the same length. Its diagonals bisect each other at right angles and bisect its angles.
A kite is a quadrilateral with two non-overlapping adjacent pairs of sides having the same length.
A trapezium is a quadrilateral having at least one pair of parallel opposite sides.
The sum of the angle measures in a quadrilateral is 360°.

content.text:
1. Our carpenter's problem is settled: two equal strips joined at their midpoints, at any angle, make a rectangle, and at right angles a square.
2. Each family has its properties: parallelograms have equal opposite sides and diagonals that bisect each other, rhombuses add perpendicular diagonals, kites have one diagonal bisecting the other at 90°, and trapeziums need one pair of parallel sides.
3. The families nest inside one another, the angles of every quadrilateral add up to 360°, and every property we used was proved, not just measured.

Puzzle Time: Which Quad?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a sheet folded into quarters gets one slanting crease across the middle corner. What shape appears when you open it?
2. The two folds are lines of symmetry, so the crease is copied in all four quarters.
3. The four copies are equal, so the shape has four equal sides: a rhombus, whose diagonals lie along the two folds.
4. Several parallel creases give rhombuses inside one another; a crease that cuts equal lengths on both folds gives equal diagonals, so a square.

content.text:
Worked example: A sheet is folded in half and then into a quarter, and one slanting crease is made across the corner at the middle of the sheet. What shape do the creases make, and how should you fold to get a square?
1. The two folds cross at right angles at the centre of the sheet.
2. Unfolding copies the crease into all four quarters, so the shape has four equal sides.
3. Its diagonals lie along the folds, so they bisect each other at right angles: a rhombus.
4. Several creases parallel to the first give rhombuses inside one another.
5. If the crease cuts off equal lengths along both folds, the diagonals are equal too, and the rhombus is a square.
Answer: A rhombus; fold the crease at 45°, cutting equal lengths on both folds, to get a square

content.question: A sheet is folded in half and then into a quarter, and one slanting crease is made across the corner at the middle of the sheet. What shape do the creases make, and how should you fold to get a square?
steps: The two folds cross at right angles at the centre of the sheet.
Unfolding copies the crease into all four quarters, so the shape has four equal sides.
Its diagonals lie along the folds, so they bisect each other at right angles: a rhombus.
Several creases parallel to the first give rhombuses inside one another.
If the crease cuts off equal lengths along both folds, the diagonals are equal too, and the rhombus is a square.
content.answer: A rhombus; fold the crease at 45°, cutting equal lengths on both folds, to get a square

If not, what is the correct relationship between these two types of quadrilaterals?
Book item: If a quadrilateral has four equal sides and one angle of 90°, will it be a square? Find the answer using geometric reasoning as well as by construction and measurement.

Book item: State whether the following statements are true or false. Justify your answers. (i) A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square. (ii) A quadrilateral having three right angles must be a rectangle. (iii) A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other must be a parallelogram. (iv) A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus. (v) A quadrilateral in which the opposite angles are equal must be a parallelogram. (vi) A quadrilateral in which all the angles are equal is a rectangle. (vii) Isosceles trapeziums are parallelograms.

Book item: A sheet is folded in half and then into a quarter, and one slanting crease is made across the corner at the middle of the sheet. What shape do the creases make, and how should you fold to get a square?
